teile.einleitung: Technocracy means that experts make decisions instead of elected politicians. They are meant to act on the basis of specialist knowledge. The idea is old and is still discussed today.
wichtigste: In a technocracy, experts decide on the basis of specialist knowledge.
Even Plato wanted those with knowledge to steer the state.
In the USA there was a technocracy movement in the 1930s.
There have been governments of experts in Italy, Greece and Austria.
Critics say that experts lack democratic legitimacy.
Independent central banks are seen as an example of technocratic power.

abschnitte.text: The word is made up of the Greek words for **skill or craft** and **rule**. In a **technocracy**, **experts** decide on the basis of specialist knowledge. They are usually appointed rather than elected. Supporters hope for good, factual decisions. Critics complain that they lack the **democratic legitimacy** that comes from elections.

The ancient philosopher **Plato** already called for rule by **philosopher kings** in his work **“The Republic”**. Those with knowledge should steer the state. This idea is regarded as an early form of technocratic thinking. In the **USA**, during the **Great Depression** of the 1930s, a movement formed around **Howard Scott**. It wanted engineers to run the economy, but soon lost importance.

In **Italy** the economics professor **Mario Monti** led a government of experts from 2011 to 2013. **Mario Draghi**, formerly President of the European Central Bank, was prime minister from 2021 to 2022. In **Greece**, **Loukas Papadimos** led a transitional government from 2011 to 2012. In **Austria**, **Brigitte Bierlein**, the first woman federal chancellor, led a government of non-party experts from 2019 to 2020.

In many democracies there are institutions that are deliberately run by experts. One example is an **independent central bank**. In Switzerland the **Swiss National Bank** decides on monetary policy independently of the government. This way specialist knowledge is meant to balance short-term political pressure.

Critics fear that political **questions of values** are presented as mere **factual questions**. Many decisions depend on what a society thinks is important. In their view, voters should decide on this. Supporters, on the other hand, argue that in crises quick and expert action is needed.

gewusst: Governments of experts often come about in times of crisis, when the parties cannot agree.
Brigitte Bierlein had previously been President of the Austrian Constitutional Court.

teile.einleitung: In 1874 Switzerland got a completely revised Federal Constitution. This total revision strengthened the Confederation and gave the people new rights. With many changes, the constitution remained in force until the end of 1999.
wichtigste: A first draft narrowly failed in 1872.
On 19 April 1874 the people and the cantons accepted the new constitution.
New was the optional referendum against federal laws.
This needed 30,000 signatures or eight cantons.
The Federal Supreme Court became a permanent court based in Lausanne.
Marriage became a matter for the state.
The constitution remained in force until the end of 1999.

abschnitte.text: On **12 May 1872** the people and the cantons **narrowly** rejected a first draft for a new constitution. Two years later a revised draft was ready. On **19 April 1874** about 340,000 men voted yes and about 198,000 no. The majority of the cantons also said yes. At that time women were not yet allowed to vote.

The new constitution brought the **optional referendum**. With it, the people could vote on **federal laws** if **30,000 signatures** were collected. Eight cantons could also call for it. In **1891** the **popular initiative for a partial revision** was added. Since then the people have been able to demand that individual articles be changed. The first successful initiative was accepted in **1893**.

Before, the **Federal Supreme Court** only met when needed. From 1874 it was a **permanent court**, and in **1875** it took up its seat in **Lausanne**. The constitution banned the **death penalty** and corporal punishment. But in **1879** the cantons were allowed to reintroduce the death penalty.

The total revision came during the **Kulturkampf** (culture struggle). In it, the liberal state tried to limit the influence of the **Catholic Church**. With **civil marriage**, marriage and civil status became a matter for the **state**. Since then a church wedding has been voluntary. The constitution also contained a stricter **ban on the Jesuits**.

The constitution of 1874 was in force for about **125 years**. During this time parts of it were changed very often. On **18 April 1999** the people and the cantons accepted a new Federal Constitution. It came into force on **1 January 2000**.

gewusst: The constitution of 1874 replaced the first Federal Constitution of 1848.
The ban on the Jesuits was only lifted in a popular vote in 1973.

teile.einleitung: Pocket money is money that children get regularly from their parents. With it they may decide for themselves what to buy or save. This way they learn early how to handle money.
wichtigste: You get pocket money regularly, for example every week.
You may decide for yourself what to spend it on.
Before buying something, you should think carefully.
You can keep your savings in a “Kässeli”.
The “Fünfliber” is the 5-franc coin.

abschnitte.text: **Pocket money** is a fixed amount that children get, for example every week or every month. The money belongs to the child. They may decide for themselves whether to buy something or save. The parents decide how much pocket money a child gets. Often the amount goes up with age.

In Switzerland a **Kässeli** is a **money box**. You collect your money in it. If you save, you can later treat yourself to something bigger. If Tim gets 2 francs every week and saves it all, he has **8 francs** after 4 weeks. Larger amounts can also be taken to a **savings account** at the bank.

Before you spend money, you should **think carefully** about whether you really want something. If you think first, you buy fewer things that you regret later. If Lea has 5 francs and buys an exercise book for 2 francs, she has **3 francs** left. Doing the sums helps you keep track.

In Switzerland you pay with **francs** and **rappen**. 100 rappen make one franc. The largest coin is the **Fünfliber**, the **5-franc coin**. There are also coins of 2 francs, 1 franc, half a franc and 20, 10 and 5 rappen.

gewusst: Many Swiss coins bear the word “Helvetia”, the Latin name for Switzerland.
Pro Juventute gives families recommendations on how much pocket money suits which age.

teile.einleitung: The agenda (in Swiss German “Traktandenliste”) shows which topics will be discussed at a meeting. In Switzerland it is best known from the municipal assembly. It is printed on the invitation that all voters receive.
wichtigste: The agenda is the list of topics for a meeting.
A single topic is called an agenda item (in German “Traktandum”).
The voters are invited to the municipal assembly.
The invitation shows the date, time and place.
The invitation comes weeks in advance so that you can prepare.
The documents are available at the municipal offices.

abschnitte.text: The **agenda** lists all the **items of business** that will be discussed at a meeting. A single topic is called an **agenda item** (in German “Traktandum”, plural “Traktanden”). The German word comes from the Latin “tractare”, which means “to deal with”. Clubs and schools also use agendas for their meetings.

The municipality sends out an **invitation** to the **municipal assembly** or announces it publicly. All **voters** are invited. The invitation shows the **date, time and place**. The agenda items are listed too. Many municipalities also put the invitation on their **website**.

The invitation comes **weeks** before the meeting. That way you have time to read about the topics and think about them. The detailed **documents** are available at the **municipal offices**, where you can read them in peace. There are often explanations from the municipal council as well.

At the meeting the agenda items are dealt with one after another. On each item you can ask questions and give your opinion. Then there is a **vote**, often by raising hands. As a rule, no decision may be made on business that is not on the agenda.

gewusst: The last agenda item is often called “Any other business”, where you can ask general questions.
It is mainly smaller municipalities that have a municipal assembly; big cities usually have a municipal parliament.

teile.einleitung: A session is the period in which the Swiss parliament sits. Each year there are four ordinary sessions of three weeks each. Sometimes parliament also holds extraordinary sittings or even meets outside Bern.
wichtigste: The spring session takes place in March, the summer session in June.
The winter session lasts from the end of November into December.
The National Council and the Council of States sit at the same time, but in separate chambers.
A quarter of the members of a chamber or the Federal Council can call for an extraordinary session.
A session outside Bern is called “extra muros”.
In May 2020 parliament met in the halls of Bernexpo because of COVID.

abschnitte.text: The parliamentary year begins with the **spring session** in **March**. In **June** comes the **summer session**, and in autumn the autumn session. The **winter session** begins at the end of November and lasts into December. After that there is a longer break until March. Each ordinary session lasts three weeks.

The **National Council** and the **Council of States** sit on the same days, but in separate chambers in the Federal Palace. That way business can pass quickly from one chamber to the other. Both chambers must approve a law for it to apply.

Sometimes urgent business has to be dealt with quickly. Then an **extraordinary session** can take place. It can be called for by a **quarter** of the members of a chamber or by the **Federal Council**. The session must concern particular items of business. When it takes place is decided by the **bureaus** of the two chambers. The bureaus also plan the chambers' work in general.

“**Extra muros**” is Latin and means “outside the walls”. This is the name for sessions that do not take place in the Federal Palace in Bern. The spring session of 2001, for example, took place in **Lugano**. Because the Parliament Building was being renovated, parliament met in **Flims** in the canton of the Grisons in autumn 2006. In May 2020 it was not possible to keep distances in the Federal Palace because of the **COVID pandemic**. That is why the extraordinary session took place in the halls of **Bernexpo**.

gewusst: During the COVID pandemic, the Swiss parliament met in exhibition halls.
Parliament has already travelled to Ticino and the Grisons to hold a session there.

teile.einleitung: Thomas Hobbes was an English philosopher of the 17th century. In his work “Leviathan” he asked why people need a state. His answer: only a strong state protects against chaos and violence.
wichtigste: Hobbes published “Leviathan” in London in 1651.
The work was written under the impression of the English Civil War.
He called the state of nature without a state a “war of all against all”.
He used the saying “Man is a wolf to man”.
For him the most important purpose of the state is security and peace.
Hobbes wanted undivided, absolute rule.

abschnitte.text: **Thomas Hobbes** lived from **1588 to 1679**. Between **1642 and 1649** the **King and Parliament** fought each other in England. This experience of chaos and violence in the **English Civil War** shaped him strongly. In **1651** he published his main work, **“Leviathan”**, in London.

Hobbes asked how people would live without a state. This imagined situation is called the **state of nature**. Without a power above them, people distrust each other and fight for survival. Hobbes called this the **“war of all against all”**. In “De Cive” he took up the saying **“Homo homini lupus”**: man is a wolf to man. According to “Leviathan”, life would be “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short”.

To escape this situation, people hand over their rights to a **sovereign**. This idea is called the **social contract**. The sovereign is meant to protect their lives. For Hobbes the most important purpose of the state is **security and peace**. The highest power must not be divided, otherwise civil war threatens again. That is why he preferred **monarchy**.

abschnitte.titel: The name and the title page
abschnitte.text: The **Leviathan** is a huge **sea monster** from the **Bible**, for example in the Book of Job. Hobbes used it as an image for the all-powerful state. The famous **title page** shows a crowned giant with a **sword and a bishop's staff**. His body is made up of many small people. This makes it visible that the sovereign unites the citizens.

gewusst: Hobbes lived to be over 90, which was very rare at the time.
Later thinkers such as John Locke and Jean-Jacques Rousseau developed the idea of the social contract further, but came to different conclusions.

teile.einleitung: Swiss Post brings letters and parcels to every home in Switzerland. Its colour is yellow and its symbol is the post horn. With the PostBus it even travels up to mountain villages.
wichtigste: Swiss Post's signature colour is yellow.
The post horn is the symbol of Swiss Post.
The yellow PostBuses also travel to remote mountain villages.
The PostBus horn plays the three notes “Tü-ta-to”.
Swiss postcodes have four digits.
A letter sent by A-Post arrives faster than one sent by B-Post.

abschnitte.text: Postboxes, delivery vans and PostBuses are **yellow**. That way you recognise Swiss Post straight away. Its symbol is the **post horn**. In the past, the coachmen of the mail coach blew the horn when the coach arrived. That way everyone knew the post was there. Swiss Post belongs to the Confederation and has its headquarters in Bern.

The yellow **PostBuses** are buses. They travel over many mountain passes and to remote villages where no train goes. The PostBus has a **three-note horn**. It sounds “Tü-ta-to” and can be heard clearly on winding mountain roads. For many people in the countryside, the PostBus is the most important link to the nearest town.

Every place has a **postcode** with **four digits**. It helps to sort letters quickly. The first digit shows the region. Bern, for example, has the postcode 3000. In the Zurich area, postcodes begin with an 8, for example 8001.

If you send a letter, you can choose. With **A-Post** the letter usually arrives on the next working day. **B-Post** takes longer but is cheaper. Letters and parcels are brought to the houses by **postwomen and postmen**. They often ride a small yellow electric vehicle.

gewusst: The PostBus “Tü-ta-to” is a set of three notes that you can hear from far away on winding mountain roads.
From the postcode you can tell which region a letter comes from.

teile.einleitung: Social assistance supports people in Switzerland who cannot pay for their own living costs. It is the last safety net of social security. The cantons and municipalities are responsible for it.
wichtigste: Social assistance only helps when your own means and insurance are not enough (**subsidiarity**).
The **basic allowance** covers food, clothes and other everyday expenses.
The rent for a suitable flat is paid on top.
The excess and the co-payment for health insurance are also paid.
Anyone who breaks their obligations can have the basic allowance reduced.
About 3 per cent of the population receive social assistance.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland there are many kinds of insurance, for example AVS, IV and unemployment insurance. If wages, savings and these insurances are not enough to live on, **social assistance** steps in. This principle is called **subsidiarity**: help is only given when you cannot help yourself. The Federal Constitution guarantees a right to help in situations of need. But social assistance is governed by the **cantons**, and the municipalities are often responsible for it.

The **basic allowance** is an amount for everyday expenses such as food, clothing, personal care and transport. **Housing costs** are calculated separately: the rent for a suitable flat is paid. If the flat is too expensive, a move can be required. On top of that come the costs of health insurance, including the **excess** and the **co-payment**. Many cantons follow the guidelines of the Swiss Conference for Social Welfare (**SKOS**).

Anyone who receives social assistance also has obligations. These include giving honest information about income and assets and making an effort to find work. Taking part in **integration measures**, for example courses or work placements, is often part of it too. Anyone who breaks their obligations through their own fault must expect a **reduction**. The basic allowance can then be cut by up to 30 per cent.

According to the Federal Statistical Office, the **social assistance rate** has been about 3 per cent for years. This means that roughly three in a hundred people receive social assistance. The share varies a lot from canton to canton and is usually higher in towns than in the countryside. **Single parents** and their children have a particularly high risk. One reason is that there is often only one wage available.

Social assistance is support during a difficult time. If someone's financial situation later improves a lot, for example through an inheritance, they can be asked to **pay it back**. Each canton sets the exact rules for this itself. Many people only receive social assistance for a short time, until they earn enough again. The aim is always for them to be able to live independently again as soon as possible.

gewusst: The right to help in situations of need is set out in Article 12 of the Federal Constitution.
Because the cantons are responsible, social assistance can look a little different from canton to canton.

teile.einleitung: Smartvote is an online voting aid from Switzerland. You answer questions on political topics, and the website shows which candidates and parties think in a similar way. But each person makes their own decision about whom to vote for.
wichtigste: Smartvote is an online voting aid.
It was used for the first time at the parliamentary elections in 2003.
It is run by the independent association Politools in Bern.
The candidates answer the same questionnaire as the voters.
The Smartspider shows political profiles on eight axes.
A recommendation from Smartvote is only a help, not an obligation.

abschnitte.text: On Smartvote you fill in a **questionnaire**. Depending on the version it has 30 to 75 questions; usually there is a short and a detailed version. Beforehand, the **candidates** answer the same questions themselves. Smartvote then compares the answers. At the end you see a list of the candidates and parties that best match your own answers.

A first public version was created in **2003** for the federal elections. Since 2004 the association **Politools** has run the voting aid. It is politically and religiously **independent** and has its headquarters in **Bern**. Since then Smartvote has been used in many elections at federal, cantonal and municipal level.

The **Smartspider** is a chart that looks like a spider's web. It has **eight axes**, one for each topic area, for example environmental protection or an open foreign policy. The further out a point lies, the more strongly you agree with that goal. This makes profiles easy to compare. The **FDP**, for example, is typically far out on the axis **liberal economic policy**, because it relies on the market and competition.

Smartvote only shows who gave **similar answers**. You do not have to vote according to the recommendation; each person has to decide for themselves. In Germany there is a similar voting aid, the **Wahl-O-Mat**. It compares the voters' positions with those of the parties. Smartvote also compares individual candidates.

gewusst: With Smartvote you can compare not only parties but also individual candidates with your own views.
The Smartspider is called that because the chart looks like a spider's web.

teile.einleitung: A special session is an extra sitting period of a chamber of the federal parliament. It helps to clear business that has piled up. The National Council in particular uses this tool regularly.
wichtigste: The federal parliament normally sits in four ordinary sessions a year.
A **special session** is used to work through unfinished business.
The **bureau** of the chamber decides whether a special session takes place.
Since 1992 a single chamber can also hold a special session on its own.
By March 2024 there had been 28 special sessions in total.
The National Council must hold a special session every year if enough business is ready.

abschnitte.text: The Federal Assembly consists of the **National Council** and the **Council of States**. The two chambers meet in **sessions**, that is, in fixed sitting periods. There are four ordinary sessions a year: in spring, summer, autumn and winter. Each lasts three weeks. Because parliament is a militia parliament, many members also have a job.

Sometimes a chamber does not manage to deal with all its business in the ordinary sessions. Then motions, reports and draft laws pile up; these are also called **pending items**. In a **special session** the chamber can work through this business. It takes place between the ordinary sessions. Whether it is needed is decided by the chamber's **bureau**, which also plans the chamber's work in general.

In the past, only both chambers together met in a special session. Since **1992** each chamber may hold a special session on its own. It is mainly the **National Council** that makes use of this. With 200 members it is much larger than the Council of States with 46 members and has more motions to deal with. The law requires the National Council to hold a special session at least once a year, as long as enough business is ready for debate.

By March 2024 there had been **28 special sessions** in total. This counts special sessions of both chambers and those of a single chamber. The National Council held a special session on its own much more often than the Council of States. A special session is usually shorter than an ordinary session. But it is just as public, and you can follow the debates on the internet.

gewusst: The National Council has more than four times as many members as the Council of States.
Besides special sessions, parliament also has extraordinary sessions, which can be called for, for example, by a quarter of the members of a chamber.

t19skhtc.t: Constitution of the Principality of Liechtenstein

teile.einleitung: The Constitution of the Principality of Liechtenstein dates from 1921. It divides power in the state between the prince and the people, a structure that hardly exists anywhere else in this form.
wichtigste: According to the constitution, Liechtenstein is a constitutional hereditary monarchy on a democratic and parliamentary basis.
The constitution dates from 5 October 1921.
In 2003 it was changed considerably in a popular vote, with about 64 per cent voting yes.
Since then the people can start a procedure to abolish the monarchy through an initiative.
The Landtag has 25 members.
In 2012 the people clearly rejected limiting the prince's right of veto.

abschnitte.text: **Article 2** calls Liechtenstein a **constitutional hereditary monarchy** on a democratic and parliamentary basis. Constitutional means that the prince is also bound by the constitution. State power lies with the **prince** and the **people** at the same time. The prince is head of state, and the office is inherited within the family. The people have strong rights such as the initiative and the referendum, similar to Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: The Landtag and the constitution of 1921
abschnitte.text: The constitution of **5 October 1921** clearly strengthened the people's rights for the first time. It is still in force today, but has been changed several times. The parliament is called the **Landtag** and has **25 members**. They are elected every four years, 15 from the Oberland and 10 from the Unterland. The Landtag passes laws, but the prince must approve them.

The princely house put forward a **popular initiative** to change the constitution. On **16 March 2003** about 64 per cent agreed. Overall, this strengthened the prince's position. But now the people can start a procedure to **abolish the monarchy** through an initiative, or bring a motion of no confidence against the prince. The Council of Europe's **Venice Commission** criticised the fact that the prince's power was growing too strong.

The prince can stop laws, and even decisions of the people, with a **veto**. A popular initiative wanted to change this in 2012. On **1 July 2012** about three quarters of voters rejected it. So the right of veto remained. Since **15 August 2004**, **Hereditary Prince Alois** has carried out the duties of head of state as deputy for his father, Prince Hans-Adam II.

gewusst: Liechtenstein uses the Swiss franc and has formed a customs union with Switzerland since 1923.
Hans-Adam II formally remains head of state, even though his son has been running the affairs of government since 2004.

teile.einleitung: A playground is a place where children can climb, slide, swing and play in the sand. Public playgrounds are open to everyone and cost nothing to get in. They are usually built and looked after by the municipality.
wichtigste: Public playgrounds often belong to the **municipality**.
You report broken play equipment to the municipality.
A covered **sandpit** stays clean.
At many playgrounds dogs are not allowed or must be kept on a lead.
At an **adventure playground** children may build and make things themselves.
An expensive new playground is often decided on by the **municipal assembly**.

abschnitte.text: A public playground is there for all children. Nobody has to pay to get in, and everyone may join in. Typical equipment includes a slide, swings, a seesaw and a climbing frame. A **climbing spider** is a net of strong ropes that looks like a spider's web. At a **water playground** there are pumps, channels and small sluices that children can use to redirect the water.

Public playgrounds usually belong to the **municipality**. Its staff check the equipment regularly and repair it. If a piece of equipment is broken, it can be dangerous. That is why you report the damage to the municipality, so that it can fix it. Under slides and swings there is often soft ground such as sand, bark chips or rubber mats, so that a fall hurts less.

So that everyone feels comfortable, there are rules. At many playgrounds **dogs** are not allowed or must be kept on a lead. That way the place stays clean and safe. A **sandpit** is often covered, because cats and other animals like to use open sand as a toilet. Rubbish goes in the bin, and you are considerate towards smaller children.

An **adventure playground** (in German “Robinsonspielplatz”) is a special playground for building and making things. There, children may build huts with wood, hammers and nails, and sometimes even make a fire. Adults look after them while they do this. The German name is a reminder of Robinson Crusoe, a character in a novel who lives alone on an island and builds everything himself. There are such playgrounds in many Swiss towns.

For a new playground, the municipality needs a piece of **land** and **money** for the equipment. A playground can cost a lot. That is why in many municipalities the people entitled to vote decide on it at the **municipal assembly**. In larger municipalities the municipal parliament decides. Sometimes children may have a say in the planning and tell what they would like.

gewusst: The German name for the adventure playground, “Robinsonspielplatz”, comes from the novel character Robinson Crusoe.
Soft ground under play equipment is called impact protection and is meant to prevent injuries when someone falls.

teile.einleitung: In tax competition, cantons and municipalities compete with their tax rates for residents and companies. It is a result of Swiss federalism. Whether it is good or bad has been debated for a long time.
wichtigste: Each canton sets its own **tax rates**.
The Federal Constitution forbids **double taxation between cantons**.
The Confederation taxes company profits at a uniform **8.5 per cent**.
In 2007 the Federal Supreme Court declared **Obwalden's** degressive tax scales unconstitutional.
With the **STAF**, tax privileges for status companies ended in 2019.
In 2023 the people accepted the **OECD minimum tax** of 15 per cent for large corporations.

abschnitte.text: Because cantons and municipalities set their own taxes, there are big differences. Some cantons try to attract companies and wealthy residents with low taxes. This is called **tax competition**. Supporters say competition forces the state to work economically. Critics fear that it means income is lost and that the gap between rich and poor grows.

According to Article 127 paragraph 3 of the Federal Constitution, the same income may not be taxed by two cantons. This **double taxation between cantons** is forbidden. The **Federal Supreme Court** set another limit in 2007: Obwalden had introduced falling tax rates for very high incomes. The court declared such **degressive scales** unconstitutional. Taxes must be based on **economic capacity**.

In 2010 the **tax fairness initiative** wanted to introduce minimum tax rates for high incomes and assets. The people and the cantons rejected it on 28 November 2010. With **lump-sum taxation**, rich foreigners who do not work in Switzerland are taxed according to their spending. Zurich was the first canton to abolish it, in 2009. In 2014 the people rejected abolishing it nationwide, with about 59 per cent voting no.

The Confederation charges a uniform **8.5 per cent** on company profits. On top of that come the very different profit taxes of the cantons and municipalities. With the **STAF**, the Federal Act on Tax Reform and AVS Financing, tax privileges for status companies ended. The people accepted it on 19 May 2019 with about 66 per cent voting yes. Since 2020 the cantons have received **21.2 per cent** instead of 17 per cent of the direct federal tax, so that they could lower their profit taxes.

There is also tax competition between countries. The **OECD**, an organisation of industrialised countries, has agreed on a minimum tax for large international corporations. It applies to companies with a turnover of over 750 million euros and is **15 per cent**. Swiss voters accepted it on 18 June 2023. For these companies, tax competition is therefore limited.

gewusst: The tax burden on the same income can be very different from canton to canton.
The STAF combined a tax reform with extra money for the AVS, hence its name.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss parliament does not meet all year round, but several times a year for a few weeks. This period is called a session. During the session, the National Council and the Council of States debate laws and vote.
wichtigste: A session is the period in which parliament sits.
There are four ordinary sessions a year.
They are called the spring, summer, autumn and winter sessions.
An ordinary session lasts about three weeks.
At the end of each session there are the final votes.
When there is a lot of business, a special session can take place.

abschnitte.text: A **session** is the period in which parliament comes together. The sessions take place in the **Parliament Building** in Bern, which is also called the Federal Palace. Only in exceptional cases has parliament sat somewhere else. Between sessions, the members go back to their work. Many have a job besides politics.

There are four **ordinary sessions**. They are named after the seasons: the **spring, summer, autumn and winter sessions**. Each lasts about **three weeks**. Together that makes 4 times 3, so 12 weeks a year. The winter session begins at the end of November and lasts into **December**. In this session parliament also elects its new presidents.

On the last Friday of a session the **final votes** take place. Then both chambers vote once and for all on the laws they have finished debating. Only when both chambers say yes is a law passed. After that, the people can still call a **referendum**.

Sometimes there is so much business that the four sessions are not enough. Then a **special session** can take place. It comes on top of the four ordinary sessions. For urgent questions there are also **extraordinary sessions**.

gewusst: The Swiss parliament only sits for about twelve weeks a year, because it is a militia parliament.
The four sessions are named after the four seasons.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss People's Party, SVP for short, is one of the big parties in Switzerland. Since 1999 it has been the party with the most votes in elections to the National Council. It is especially committed to Switzerland's independence.
wichtigste: The SVP was founded in 1971, mainly from the Farmers, Trades and Citizens' Party (BGB).
Its colour is green, and its logo shows a bright yellow sun.
Since 1999 it has been the party with the most votes in Switzerland.
Its best result was 29.4 per cent in 2015.
It is against Switzerland joining the EU.
In 2025 Guy Parmelin and Albert Rösti sat on the Federal Council for the SVP.

abschnitte.text: The SVP has its roots in the **Farmers, Trades and Citizens' Party**, BGB for short. The Bernese farmer **Rudolf Minger** was the first BGB politician to be elected to the Federal Council, in 1929. In 1971 the BGB merged with the Democratic Parties of the cantons of Glarus and the Grisons. This is how the SVP came about. The **green logo** with a yellow sun is a reminder of its farming roots.

For a long time the SVP was a rather small party in the Federal Council. In the 1990s it grew strongly. In the elections of **1999** it won 22.5 per cent and came ahead of the SP and the FDP for the first time. Since then it has been the **party with the most votes** without a break. Its record result came in **2015** with 29.4 per cent. That is the highest share of any party since proportional representation was introduced.

The SVP is seen as **right-wing conservative**. It stands for an independent Switzerland and is against **joining the EU**. Important topics for it are immigration, neutrality and low taxes. It often brings its concerns to the people with popular initiatives. The **deportation initiative** was accepted on 28 November 2010. Other initiatives, such as the limitation initiative, were rejected. Opponents criticise its positions, while supporters value it as a clear voice.

The SVP has two members on the Federal Council. In 2025 these were **Guy Parmelin**, in office since 2016, and **Albert Rösti**, since 2023. Rösti followed Ueli Maurer, who stepped down at the end of 2022. Since 2024 the president of the SVP Switzerland has been **Marcel Dettling** from the canton of Schwyz. He followed Marco Chiesa.

gewusst: With 29.4 per cent in 2015, the SVP reached the highest share of the vote of any party since proportional representation was introduced.
The sun in the SVP logo and the green colour are reminders of its origins as a farmers' party.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Civil Code, ZGB for short, governs many everyday matters between people. For example, it decides when you come of age, who owns a thing and who inherits after someone dies. It has applied throughout Switzerland since 1912.
wichtigste: The Civil Code was written by the lawyer Eugen Huber.
It was passed in 1907 and has applied since 1 January 1912.
Under the Civil Code you come of age at 18.
Inheritance law governs who inherits.
Property law governs ownership and possession.
Article 2 requires people to act in good faith.
Turkey adopted the Civil Code almost completely in 1926.

abschnitte.titel: One law for all of Switzerland
abschnitte.text: In the past, every canton had its own **private law**. Private law governs relations between people, for example when buying, inheriting or within the family. On behalf of the Confederation, the lawyer **Eugen Huber** wrote a draft for a shared law. Parliament passed the Civil Code in **1907**. It came into force on **1 January 1912**. Eugen Huber is therefore regarded as the father of the Civil Code.

The **law of persons** says, for example, when you **come of age**. According to Article 14, you are of age once you have reached the age of 18. Until 1996 the limit was still 20. **Family law** governs, among other things, marriage and the relationship between parents and children.

**Inheritance law** governs who receives someone's assets after they die. It also decides when a **will** is valid and what **compulsory share** close relatives receive. **Property law** decides who owns a thing or a piece of land and how you acquire ownership. This also includes the **land register**, in which all plots of land are recorded.

Article 1 allows the court something special: if there is neither a law nor customary law, it decides according to the rule it would make **as legislator**. This article is regarded as very modern. Article 2 requires everyone to act in **good faith**, that is, honestly and fairly. Obvious abuse of a right is not protected.

The Civil Code is written clearly and is easy to understand. That is why it also served other countries as a model. **Turkey** adopted it almost completely in 1926 when it modernised its law. For this, it was translated into Turkish.

gewusst: A Swiss code of law became almost completely the law of Turkey in 1926.
Until 1996 you only came of age in Switzerland at 20.

teile.einleitung: The rules of a game set out how it is played and who wins. If everyone knows the same rules, a game is fair. Rules are also important in living together and in democracy.
wichtigste: Rules make sure that everyone plays the same way.
In **chess**, White always starts.
In **rock, paper, scissors**, scissors cut paper.
A Swiss game of **Jass** is played with 36 cards.
In **Mensch ärgere dich nicht** you need a six to bring a piece into play.
In **football** only the goalkeeper may pick the ball up with their hands.

abschnitte.text: Without rules, nobody would know what is allowed and who has won. If everyone knows the **rules of the game**, everyone plays by the same rules. That way the game is **fair**. That is why it is best to explain the rules before the game. Sometimes people also agree together to change a rule so that it suits everyone.

In **chess**, the player with the white pieces always makes the first move. After that, the two take turns. In **Mensch ärgere dich nicht**, a board game similar to Ludo, a piece may only leave its home and move onto the board with a six. After a six you may roll again. Fixed rules like these make every game exciting, because everyone has the same chances.

**Jass** is one of the most popular card games in Switzerland. A Swiss pack of Jass cards has 36 cards in four suits. In **rock, paper, scissors**, two people show a sign with their hand at the same time. Scissors cut paper, rock blunts scissors, and paper wraps up rock. So every sign can win and lose.

In **hide-and-seek** (in Swiss German “Versteckis”), the seeker counts with their eyes closed while the others hide. Only then do they start to search. In **tag** (in Swiss German “Fangis”), the catcher tries to touch another child. That child then becomes the new catcher. In **football**, only the goalkeeper may play the ball with their hands, in their own penalty area.

In big games a **referee** makes sure that everyone keeps to the rules. In everyday life there are rules too, for example at school, in traffic or at the playground. In a democracy the most important rules, the laws, are decided together. Parliament or the people can also change them again. As in a game: rules are fair when they apply equally to everyone.

gewusst: In chess, White has 20 possible first moves.
For Jass there are two kinds of cards in Switzerland: German cards with bells, shields, roses and acorns, and French cards with hearts, diamonds, spades and clubs.

teile.einleitung: An ordinance is a legal rule that is usually issued by the government. It sets out the details of how a law is put into practice in everyday life.
wichtigste: Most federal ordinances are issued by the Federal Council.
In the hierarchy, ordinances are below the constitution and laws.
Every ordinance needs a basis in the constitution or a law.
There is no referendum against ordinances.
Important rules such as the main features of taxes must be in a law.
In serious crises the Federal Council may issue temporary emergency ordinances.

abschnitte.text: At the very top is the **Federal Constitution**. Below it come the **federal laws**, which parliament passes. One level lower again are the **ordinances**. A lower level may never contradict a higher one. So an ordinance must keep to the law and the constitution.

A law sets out the important **principles**. The ordinance governs the **details**, for example forms, time limits or technical values. The **Federal Council** may only issue ordinances if the constitution or a law gives it the power to do so. It can hand over simple technical rules to a **department**. These are then called departmental ordinances.

The people can call a **referendum** against federal laws, but not against ordinances. That is why, according to the Federal Constitution, important rules must be set out in a **law**. These include, for example, the main features of **taxes**: who has to pay them and how much. Because neither the National Council nor the Council of States has to agree, an ordinance can be changed much **faster**. The **Federal Assembly** can also issue ordinances itself, for example on its own organisation.

In serious crises the Federal Council may issue **emergency ordinances** directly on the basis of the constitution. These must be **temporary**. This is meant to let the state act quickly when there is no time for a law. This happened, for example, in **2020** during the **COVID-19 pandemic**. At that time the Federal Council used ordinances to close schools and many shops, among other things.

gewusst: All federal laws and ordinances in force are in the Classified Compilation of Federal Legislation, SR for short.
There are many more ordinances than laws, because they govern the many details.

teile.einleitung: Freedom of assembly is a fundamental right. It allows everyone to meet peacefully with others, for example at a rally, and to show their opinion there together.
wichtigste: Freedom of assembly is set out in Art. 22 of the Federal Constitution.
You may organise meetings, take part in them or stay away from them.
Only peaceful assemblies are protected.
Rallies on public land usually need a permit from the municipality or canton.
Restrictions need a legal basis and must be proportionate.
Before 1999, freedom of assembly was regarded as an unwritten fundamental right.

abschnitte.text: A **rally** or **demonstration** is a public gathering for a cause. People show there together what they are for or against. **Art. 22** of the Federal Constitution protects the right to **organise** assemblies, to **take part** in them or to **stay away** from them. So nobody has to join in a rally. The European Convention on Human Rights also protects this right.

Fundamental and human rights expressly protect only **peaceful** assemblies. Anyone who uses violence cannot rely on freedom of assembly. It should be distinguished from **freedom of association** in **Art. 23**. That protects the founding of clubs and parties. Freedom of assembly, on the other hand, concerns individual gatherings.

Streets and squares are used by everyone. A demonstration uses them more heavily than usual; this is called **enhanced common use**. That is why **municipalities and cantons** may require a **permit** and set conditions, for example on place and time. In cities such as Zurich or Bern, the city administration usually grants the permit. One well-known place is the **Bundesplatz**, right in front of the Federal Palace in Bern.

The state may only restrict an assembly under certain conditions. According to **Art. 36** there must be a **legal basis** and a **public interest**, and the measure must be **proportionate**. A ban is only allowed if milder conditions are not enough. Even before 1999 the **Federal Supreme Court** recognised freedom of assembly as an **unwritten fundamental right**. With the new Federal Constitution it was written down expressly.

gewusst: Freedom of assembly also includes the right to stay away: nobody may be forced to take part in a rally.
Rallies on the Bundesplatz in Bern need a permit from the city of Bern.

teile.einleitung: The polling station is the place where you can vote in person on voting Sunday. Here you hand in your ballot paper and put it in the ballot box. That is why people say “going to the ballot box”.
wichtigste: At the polling station you can vote in person on voting Sunday.
It is often in the municipal building or in a school.
Members of the electoral office make sure that everything runs properly.
You show your voting card before you vote.
A booth or a screen protects the secrecy of the ballot.
Campaigning for yes or no is not allowed at the polling station.
Each person may only vote once, even if they have already voted by post.

abschnitte.text: Each municipality decides where its **polling station** is. It is often in the **municipal building** or in a **school**, because everyone knows these places well. Big cities have several polling stations in different districts. Where you can go is usually printed on the voting papers.

On **voting Sunday**, polling stations are usually only open in the **morning**. In some municipalities you can also go on the Saturday or on another day beforehand. When the polling station closes, the **counting** of the votes begins. The results then become known in the afternoon or evening.

If you want to vote, you take your **voting card** with you. The members of the **electoral office** check it. This shows that you are entitled to vote. Then you fill in your ballot paper behind a **screen** or in a booth. Finally you put it in the sealed **ballot box**.

At the polling station everyone should be able to decide in peace. That is why nobody may **campaign** there for yes or no. The screen makes sure that nobody is watching. This keeps the **secrecy of the ballot**. Each voter has only **one vote** per proposal.

Today most people in Switzerland vote **by post**. But the polling station remains important for everyone who likes to vote in person. Anyone who has already voted by post may not vote again at the polling station. Otherwise the result would be distorted.

gewusst: The expression “going to the ballot box” is often used even when someone votes by post.
The members of the electoral office are usually people from the municipality itself who take on this task.

teile.einleitung: Clean streets and squares make a municipality nicer and safer. The municipality's staff take care of this with brooms and machines. But all residents can help too.
wichtigste: The municipality's public works service or depot keeps the streets clean.
The road sweeper cleans streets and pavements with rotating brushes.
In autumn a particularly large amount of leaves is cleared away.
At the Robidog there are little bags for dog poo.
Anyone who puts rubbish in the bin saves the municipality work and money.
On Clean-up Day many people collect rubbish voluntarily.

abschnitte.text: In a municipality the **public works service** or **depot** is usually responsible for cleanliness. The staff sweep streets, squares and pavements. They also empty the public **litter bins**, for example at bus stops. Otherwise full bins would overflow.

For large areas there is the **road sweeper**, also called a **sweeping machine**. It has **rotating brushes** that sweep up dust, leaves and rubbish. A vacuum sucks the dirt into a container. The machine often sprays a little water as it goes, so that less dust is stirred up.

In **autumn** lots of leaves fall from the trees. Wet **leaves** can be slippery and are therefore cleared away. After a **village festival** there is often a lot of rubbish lying around. Then the municipality or helpers usually clean up **the very next day**.

The green **Robidog** is known all over Switzerland. Little **bags** for dog poo hang on it. Dog owners use them to pick up their dog's poo and put the bag in the box. That way paths and meadows stay clean.

If nobody throws rubbish on the ground, the municipality stays clean. Dropping rubbish outdoors is called **littering**. In many places there is a **fine** for it. On **Clean-up Day** many people voluntarily collect rubbish in nature and in the municipality, and school classes take part too.

gewusst: The Robidog was invented in Switzerland.
In winter the public works service also clears snow and spreads salt or grit so that nobody slips.

teile.einleitung: An electoral threshold is a hurdle in proportional elections. Parties that receive less than a certain share of the votes get no seats in parliament. Many countries have such hurdles; Switzerland does not in the National Council elections.
wichtigste: A threshold is meant to prevent a **fragmented parliament**.
In Germany the **five per cent hurdle** applies in elections to the Bundestag.
With three directly won seats, a party still gets into the Bundestag (as of 2025).
Parties of national minorities such as the **SSW** are exempt from the hurdle.
Since 2014 Israel has had a hurdle of 3.25 per cent.
In Switzerland a **natural hurdle** arises in small cantons.

abschnitte.text: In a **proportional election**, parties receive as many seats as their share of the votes. Without a hurdle, a great many small parties could enter parliament. Then it is difficult to form stable majorities and a government that can act. An **electoral threshold** is meant to prevent this. Critics, on the other hand, say that this means many votes have no effect.

In elections to the Bundestag, a party needs at least **5 per cent** of the second votes. But if it wins at least three constituencies directly, it is still counted according to its share of the votes. In 2024 the Federal Constitutional Court let this **basic mandate clause** continue to apply until new rules are made. Parties of national minorities, such as the **South Schleswig Voters' Association** of the Danish minority and the Frisians, are exempt from the hurdle. In 2025 the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance missed getting in by a very narrow margin with 4.981 per cent.

In Germany there is no threshold for elections to the European Parliament. In 2014 the Federal Constitutional Court declared the three per cent hurdle unconstitutional. It found that the parties' equal opportunities were violated, because the European Parliament does not have to support a government. That is why even very small parties from Germany enter the European Parliament. Other countries have their own rules for European elections.

In **Israel** the hurdle was raised step by step, most recently in 2014 from 2 to 3.25 per cent. Even so, more than ten parties usually sit in the Knesset, the Israeli parliament. **Turkey** had a hurdle of 10 per cent for decades, one of the highest in Europe. In 2022 it was lowered to 7 per cent. A calculation shows the effect: if parties below the hurdle together receive 15 per cent, a party with 42.5 per cent of the votes gets half of the seats, because 42.5 divided by 85 gives 0.5.

In the **National Council elections** there is no threshold set by law. But each canton is a separate constituency with a fixed number of seats. In small cantons only a few seats are shared out. A list there needs a high share of the votes to win a seat at all. This is called a **natural** or **de facto hurdle**.

gewusst: Although Israel has an electoral threshold, there are often more than ten parties in the Knesset.
In cantons with only one National Council seat, the person with the most votes simply wins.

teile.einleitung: Criminal law sets out which acts are forbidden and what punishment they can bring. In Switzerland the most important rules are in the Swiss Criminal Code. The state prosecutes and punishes such acts.
wichtigste: Criminal law says which acts the state punishes.
The Swiss Criminal Code has applied since 1 January 1942.
Before that, each canton had its own criminal law.
Offences prosecuted on complaint are only pursued if the injured person files a complaint.
Offences prosecuted ex officio are pursued by the authorities on their own initiative.
Monetary penalties are calculated in daily rates.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss Criminal Code**, StGB for short, was passed in **1937**. It came into force on **1 January 1942**. Before that, each **canton** had its own criminal law. Since then the same rules about what is a crime have applied throughout Switzerland.

Criminal law is meant to **protect** people and their property. It describes precisely which behaviour is forbidden. An important principle is: **no punishment without law**. So you may only be punished if the act was already set out in law as a crime beforehand. Until there is a verdict, every accused person is considered **innocent**.

With an **offence prosecuted on complaint**, the injured person must file a **criminal complaint**, for example in the case of simple damage to property. Without a complaint the act is not pursued. With an **offence prosecuted ex officio**, the police and the public prosecutor's office must act as soon as they learn about it. This applies to serious acts such as **robbery**. No complaint is needed for this.

The law has different penalties, such as the **fine**, the **monetary penalty** and the **prison sentence**. The monetary penalty is calculated in **daily rates**. The court decides the number of daily rates according to how serious the act is. The amount of a daily rate depends on **income**. That way the penalty hits poor and rich people about equally hard.
Children and young people have their own **juvenile criminal law**. It relies above all on **education** and protection. Young people should learn to take responsibility and find a good path again.

gewusst: In Switzerland children under 10 cannot be punished.
Since 2011 a uniform Criminal Procedure Code has applied throughout Switzerland, setting out how criminal proceedings work.

teile.einleitung: In the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden, people vote in the open air at the Landsgemeinde. There, men may show a side arm instead of a paper identity card. A side arm is a bladed weapon that you wear at your side, for example a sword or a sabre.
wichtigste: In Appenzell Innerrhoden the side arm counts as a voting card for men.
Swords, sabres and bayonets count as side arms.
A sword of this kind has a long, narrow blade.
Many swords are passed down in the family.
Women, and men too, can show the paper voting card.

abschnitte.text: A **side arm** is not a firearm but a **bladed weapon**. You wear it in a sheath on your belt at the hip, that is, at your side. A **sword** of this kind has a long, narrow metal blade. The **sabre** and the **bayonet** also count. A bayonet is a blade that can also be fixed onto a rifle.

abschnitte.titel: The voting card at the Landsgemeinde
abschnitte.text: At the **Landsgemeinde** in Appenzell Innerrhoden, the people entitled to vote gather in a square and vote by raising their hands. There, men may show their side arm as a **voting card**. Women show the paper voting card. Men may also use this card. Many swords are passed on by a father or grandfather and are a valuable **heirloom**.

In the past, it was mainly the men who **defended** the land in war who were allowed to have a say. The weapon therefore showed that someone was a full citizen and could take part in decisions. Today the side arm is above all a **tradition**. It is a reminder of the long history of the Landsgemeinde.

gewusst: In Appenzell Innerrhoden an old family sword can serve as a card for voting.
Despite its German name, which contains the word for “gun”, the side arm is not a firearm but a blade.

teile.einleitung: Compulsory voting means that you have to take part in votes and elections. In Switzerland there is no general duty to vote; voting is voluntary. One exception with a long history is the canton of Schaffhausen, where compulsory voting still applies today.
wichtigste: Compulsory voting means that you have to vote and elect.
In Switzerland voting is voluntary as a rule.
The canton of Schaffhausen has compulsory voting with a long tradition.
Anyone there who does not vote without a good reason has to pay a small fine.
In the past other cantons also had compulsory voting.
Countries such as Belgium, Australia and Brazil have compulsory voting in elections.

abschnitte.text: With **compulsory voting**, all voters must take part in votes and elections. You do not have to say yes or no; you may also hand in a blank paper. All that matters is that you take part. Anyone who stays away without an excuse is punished, usually with a small fine.

In Switzerland taking part in federal votes is **voluntary**. Nobody is punished for not voting. That is why **turnout** is often only about 40 to 50 per cent. But on important or controversial topics, a lot more people go to the ballot box.

In the canton of **Schaffhausen**, compulsory voting has applied since the 19th century. Anyone who does not vote and has no reason for it has to pay a fine of 6 francs. This duty applies to votes and elections in the canton and at federal level too. That is why turnout in Schaffhausen is usually higher than in the rest of Switzerland.

In the past, several cantons had compulsory voting, for example at the Landsgemeinden. Anyone who did not turn up could be punished. Over time almost all cantons abolished this duty again. Only Schaffhausen has kept it to this day.

Around the world some countries have **compulsory voting in elections**, such as Belgium, Luxembourg, Australia and Brazil. Supporters say that this way everyone's opinion is counted. Opponents think that freedom also includes not voting. This question is discussed again and again in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: The duty to take part in votes and elections.
The share of voters who have voted.
A money penalty for breaking a rule in a small way.
A container into which you put your ballot paper.

gewusst: Because of compulsory voting, Schaffhausen often has the highest turnout of all cantons in federal votes.
The fine of 6 francs is so small that it is more about the signal than about the money.
Australia introduced compulsory voting as early as 1924.

teile.einleitung: Tax liability means that a person or company has to pay taxes. Anyone who lives or works in Switzerland is usually liable to pay tax. How much you pay depends on income, assets and where you live.
wichtigste: Anyone who lives in Switzerland is usually **liable to pay tax** here.
For taxes, what usually counts is where you live on **31 December**.
An apprentice's wage is taxed **to the apprentice themselves**.
With **tax progression**, the tax rate rises with income.
With **tax at source**, the tax is deducted directly from the wage.
Anyone who declares their assets correctly gets the **withholding tax** of 35 per cent back.
If you do not hand in a tax return, the tax office makes an assessment.

abschnitte.text: Anyone whose **place of residence** is in Switzerland is usually liable to pay tax here. What counts is your place of residence at the end of the tax period, that is, on **31 December**. If you move to another canton in the autumn, you pay the taxes for the whole year in the new canton. Because each canton sets its own tax rates, you pay different amounts depending on the canton. In most cantons, members of a recognised **national church** also pay a **church tax**.

The **earned income** of minors is taxed separately from their parents. A 16-year-old apprentice therefore pays tax on their wage themselves. Depending on the canton and the size of the wage, they fill in their own **tax return**. At the latest from the year in which you turn 18, you usually have to hand in a tax return yourself. In it you state your income and assets.

With **tax progression** you pay a higher percentage on higher incomes. So people who earn little pay not only fewer francs but also a smaller share. This way people with a lot of income contribute more to the state's tasks. VAT affects everyone too: if a toy costs 100 francs without tax, it costs **108.10 francs** with 8.1 per cent VAT. But this tax is the same for everyone, no matter how much you earn.

With **tax at source**, the employer deducts the tax directly from the wage. It applies mainly to foreign employees without a settlement permit, that is, without a C permit. The **withholding tax** is 35 per cent and is deducted, for example, from interest on savings accounts. Anyone who declares their savings correctly in their tax return gets it back. So it pays to be honest.

abschnitte.titel: When the tax return is missing
abschnitte.text: Anyone who does not hand in their tax return despite a reminder is assessed **at the tax office's discretion**. This means the tax office estimates income and assets itself. A **fine** can also be imposed. The estimate often turns out rather high. That is why it is wiser to hand in your tax return on time.

gewusst: The withholding tax is so high so that it pays to declare your savings honestly.
If you move on 31 December, you pay the whole year's taxes at your new place of residence.

teile.einleitung: The tax multiplier (in German “Steuerfuss”) decides how much tax you pay to your municipality or canton. It is a percentage of what is called the simple tax. Each municipality sets its own tax multiplier every year.
wichtigste: The **tax multiplier** is a percentage of the **simple tax**.
The simple tax comes from the cantonal tax scale.
With a tax multiplier of **100 per cent** you pay exactly the simple tax.
The tax multiplier is set **every year**, usually together with the budget.
In municipalities without a parliament, the **municipal assembly** decides.
It applies mainly to income tax and wealth tax.

abschnitte.text: First the tax office works out the **simple tax** from income and assets. For this, the canton's tax scale applies. Then the simple tax is multiplied by the **tax multiplier**. With a tax multiplier of 100 per cent you pay exactly the simple tax. If it is higher, you pay more; if it is lower, you pay less.

If the simple tax is 2000 francs and the tax multiplier is 110 per cent, you calculate 2000 times 1.1. That gives **2200 francs** of municipal tax. With 3000 francs of simple tax and a tax multiplier of 95 per cent, you calculate 3000 times 0.95, so **2850 francs**. If a municipality raises the tax multiplier from 100 to 120 per cent, the tax on 1500 francs of simple tax goes up by **300 francs**. So just a few percentage points make a noticeable amount of money.

In municipalities without a parliament, the voters set the tax multiplier at the **municipal assembly**. In municipalities with a parliament, the **parliament** usually does this. The cantons also set their own tax multiplier. The tax multiplier is decided **every year**, usually together with the **budget**. That way the canton and the municipality can respond to their financial situation.

The tax multiplier applies mainly to **income tax** and **wealth tax**. VAT and customs duties, on the other hand, belong to the Confederation. Because each municipality decides for itself, tax multipliers are very different. Anyone who lives in a municipality with a low tax multiplier pays less tax on the same income. Municipalities with many tasks or little income often need a higher tax multiplier.

gewusst: With a tax multiplier of 100 per cent, the simple tax and the municipal tax are exactly the same.
Two neighbouring municipalities can have very different tax multipliers.

teile.einleitung: Subsidiarity means that a task should be carried out at the lowest sensible level. What the municipality can solve well itself should not be done by the canton, and what the canton can solve should not be done by the Confederation. This principle is an important part of how the Swiss state is built.
wichtigste: Subsidiarity means that tasks are carried out at the lowest sensible level.
In Switzerland there are three levels: municipality, canton and Confederation.
The higher level only helps if the lower one cannot manage a task alone.
The principle of subsidiarity has been in the Federal Constitution since 2008.
The word comes from the Latin “subsidium” and means help.
The European Union also has the principle of subsidiarity.

abschnitte.text: The word **subsidiarity** comes from the Latin “subsidium”, which means help or support. The idea is that the larger community should only help when the smaller one cannot carry out a task itself. So first it is up to the people themselves, the family and the municipality. Only after that come the canton and the Confederation.

Switzerland has three **levels of the state**: about 2100 municipalities, 26 cantons and the Confederation. The municipalities look after things such as nursery schools, primary schools, rubbish and local roads. The cantons are responsible, among other things, for the police, hospitals and grammar schools. The Confederation governs what has to be the same for the whole country, such as the army, foreign policy and money.

Since 2008 the principle has been set out expressly in Article 5a of the **Federal Constitution**. It says that the principle of subsidiarity must be respected when state tasks are assigned and carried out. It was added with the reform of financial equalisation between the Confederation and the cantons. But the principle had been practised in Switzerland for much longer.

The municipality often knows the local problems better than the Confederation in Bern. Solutions can therefore be better suited to the people. Citizens can have a say more closely, for example at the **municipal assembly**. This also leads to differences between cantons, for example in school holidays or taxes.

The term became well known especially through Catholic **social teaching**, above all through a papal letter from 1931. Later the European Union also took it into its treaties. There, the EU should only act if the member states cannot achieve a goal well enough on their own. Germany and Austria also have the principle in how their states are built.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tasks are carried out as far down as possible.
Municipality, canton or Confederation.
Dividing power between the federal level and the member states.
Rich cantons and the Confederation help poorer cantons with money.

gewusst: Because the cantons are responsible for schools, the summer holidays in Switzerland do not start on the same day everywhere.
Most of the taxes that Swiss people pay go to the canton and the municipality, not to the Confederation.
The number of municipalities falls every year because of mergers.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss cross is a white cross on a red background. It is the best-known symbol of Switzerland and appears on the flag, on the passport and on many products. The Swiss flag has a special shape: it is square.
wichtigste: The Swiss cross is white and stands free on a red background.
On land the Swiss flag is square.
Only Switzerland and Vatican City have a square flag.
On ships the Swiss flag is rectangular.
The symbol of the Red Cross is the Swiss flag with the colours swapped.
On 1 August many people hang out the flag.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss flag is **square**, which means it is as high as it is wide. That is very rare for national flags. Only **Vatican City** also has a square flag. The white cross stands **free in the middle** and does not touch the edge. On **ships**, however, a rectangular Swiss flag flies, as is usual everywhere on the water.

On **1 August** Switzerland celebrates its national day. Many people then hang the flag on their house or balcony. That way they show they are joining in the celebrations. On this day you also often see the Swiss cross on paper lanterns, napkins and cakes.

Many products carry the Swiss cross. It shows that they come **from Switzerland**. The cross is seen as a sign of quality. That is why there are rules: not every product may simply carry the cross; it must really come largely from Switzerland.

The **Red Cross** is an aid organisation that was founded in Switzerland. It was **Henry Dunant** from Geneva who inspired its founding. For this he received the first **Nobel Peace Prize** in 1901. In honour of Switzerland, its flag with the **colours swapped** was chosen as the symbol: a red cross on a white background.

gewusst: In the whole world only two countries have a square flag: Switzerland and Vatican City.
The symbol of the Red Cross is a reversed Swiss flag.

teile.einleitung: The treaty referendum is a people's right in Switzerland that lets the people vote on international treaties. Switzerland concludes such treaties with other countries or international organisations. For particularly important treaties, the people have the last word under certain conditions.
wichtigste: With the treaty referendum, the people can vote on international treaties.
A treaty is an agreement between states.
There is a mandatory and an optional treaty referendum.
When joining certain organisations, the people must always vote.
An optional treaty referendum needs 50,000 signatures in 100 days or eight cantons.
The treaty referendum has existed since 1921.

abschnitte.text: A **treaty** is a binding agreement between two or more states. It can be about trade, transport, taxes, environmental protection or police cooperation, for example. For Switzerland, the Federal Council signs such treaties. Important treaties must then be approved by parliament.

For particularly important treaties the people must always vote; this is the **mandatory** treaty referendum. It applies to joining organisations for collective security or supranational communities. Then a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons are needed. A well-known example is the vote on the European Economic Area, **EEA** for short, in 1992, which the people narrowly rejected.

Other important treaties are subject to the **optional** referendum. These include treaties that are unlimited in time and cannot be terminated, that provide for joining an international organisation or that contain important legal rules. Anyone who wants a vote must collect 50,000 signatures in 100 days, or eight cantons must call for it. Then a majority of the people is enough.

The treaty referendum was introduced in 1921, at first only for very long treaties. It was later extended in 1977 and 2003. This was a response to the fact that more and more important rules are set out in international treaties. That way **direct democracy** is kept in foreign policy too.

In 2005 the people voted on the **Schengen** and Dublin agreements and accepted them. There was also a vote on the Bilateral Agreements with the European Union in 2000. Such votes are often fiercely debated. They show how important the relationship with the EU is for Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A binding agreement between states.
Standing above the individual states, like the European Union.
States protect themselves together, for example in an alliance.
Parliament's agreement to a treaty.

gewusst: The EEA was rejected in 1992 by a very narrow margin, with about 50.3 per cent voting no.
Switzerland has concluded several thousand treaties with other states, but only a few of them were put to a vote.

teile.einleitung: The presumption of innocence is an important principle under the rule of law. Anyone accused of a crime is considered innocent until a court has convicted them with a final judgement.
wichtigste: Every person is considered innocent until they are convicted with a final judgement.
In Switzerland the presumption of innocence is set out in Article 32 of the Federal Constitution.
Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights also protects it.
The authorities must prove guilt; the accused person does not have to prove their innocence.
“In dubio pro reo” means: when in doubt, in favour of the accused.
Even someone in pre-trial detention is still considered innocent.

abschnitte.text: If someone is suspected of having committed a crime, that is not yet proof. The person is considered **innocent** until a court convicts them with a **final** judgement. Final means that the judgement can no longer be challenged. This is the case when the time limit for an appeal has run out or the highest court has decided. In this way the principle protects everyone from hasty punishment.

In Switzerland the presumption of innocence is set out in **Article 32 of the Federal Constitution**. The **Criminal Procedure Code** also names this principle. On top of that comes **Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights**, by which Switzerland is bound. It guarantees a fair trial. The UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights also contains the presumption of innocence.

The **criminal prosecution authorities**, that is, the police and the public prosecutor's office, must prove guilt. The accused person does not have to prove their innocence. Closely linked to this is the Latin phrase **“in dubio pro reo”**. It means: when in doubt, in favour of the accused. If real doubts about guilt remain, the court must acquit the person.

Sometimes someone is held in **pre-trial detention** before the verdict. This is not a punishment, but is meant, for example, to prevent escape or the covering up of evidence. The person is therefore still considered innocent. Newspapers and news reports also respect the principle. They write about an **“alleged” offender** as long as there is only a suspicion.

gewusst: The presumption of innocence applies only to the state and the court, but the media should still not prejudge anyone.
The phrase “in dubio pro reo” comes from Latin and is still used in courts today.

teile.einleitung: After an election, all the votes have to be counted precisely. Only then is it clear who has been elected. In a National Council election this is a lot of work, because there are many names and lists.
wichtigste: In the National Council election the counting happens on **election Sunday**.
Counting an election takes longer than counting a vote on an issue.
The **computer** helps to add up the votes.
The votes of registered **Swiss citizens abroad** are counted too.
Ballot papers with insults are **invalid**.
The final result shows how many **seats** each party gets.

abschnitte.text: The National Council is elected every four years in October. Many voters vote by post; others go to the ballot box on Sunday. After the ballot boxes close on **election Sunday**, the counting begins. The **polling stations' electoral offices** in the municipalities are responsible for it. Many results are already available in the evening.

abschnitte.titel: Many names, a lot of work
abschnitte.text: In a vote on an issue you only count yes and no. A National Council election is more complicated. You choose a **list**, but you can cross out names, add names from other lists (**panachage**) or write a name twice (**cumulation**). All these votes for people and lists have to be recorded. That is why counting an election takes longer.

The votes on the ballot papers are recorded and then added up by **computer**. This makes the results come faster. The municipalities report their figures to the canton. The votes of **Swiss citizens living abroad** who have registered are also counted in their voting canton. In the end, a result is worked out for each canton.

Not every ballot paper counts. A paper with **defamatory remarks**, that is, insults, is **invalid**. Papers that have not been filled in correctly can also be invalid. Invalid papers are not taken into account in the count. That is why it pays to fill in your ballot paper carefully.

On election evening, **television**, **radio** and the **internet** report on the results live. The Confederation and the cantons also publish the figures online. After the count it is clear how many **seats** each party gets in each canton. After that, it is decided which people on the lists are elected. These are the ones with the most personal votes on their list.

gewusst: In the National Council election you can write the same name twice on the ballot paper; this is called cumulation.
The seats are first shared out among the lists and only after that among the people.

teile.einleitung: The right to vote is the right to help decide in elections and votes. In Switzerland all Swiss citizens who are at least 18 years old have it. They are called voters.
wichtigste: With the right to vote, you can elect and vote.
Swiss citizens who are of age are entitled to vote.
Since 1991 the federal voting age has been 18.
Women have only had the right to vote at federal level since 1971.
The voting card shows that you are allowed to vote.
In the canton of Glarus you can vote from the age of 16.
Swiss citizens living abroad also have the right to vote at federal level.

abschnitte.titel: What is the right to vote?
abschnitte.text: The **right to vote** is one of the political rights. Anyone who has it may say yes or no in votes and choose people in elections. They may also sign popular initiatives and referendums. Being able to be elected to an office yourself is called the **right to stand for election**, which is closely linked to it.

At federal level, all **voters** who have Swiss citizenship and are 18 years old take part. Foreign residents may not vote at federal level. But in some cantons, such as Neuchâtel and Jura, they may have a say in the municipality. Swiss citizens who live abroad may also take part in federal votes.

Before every vote you receive the papers at home by post. They include the **voting card**, a paper that shows that you are allowed to vote. You have to sign it and hand it in together with the ballot paper. This prevents anyone from voting more than once.

For a long time only men were allowed to vote in Switzerland. Only on 7 February 1971 did the men accept **votes for women** at federal level. The last canton was Appenzell Innerrhoden, which had to introduce it in 1990 on the orders of the Federal Supreme Court. This made Switzerland one of the last countries in Europe.

Until 1991 the federal voting age was 20. Then the people agreed to lower it to **18**. In 2007 the canton of Glarus became the only canton to introduce a voting age of 16 for cantonal and municipal votes. There were votes on this in other cantons, but the proposals were mostly rejected.

begriffe.erklaerung: People who are allowed to help make political decisions.
A paper that shows that you are allowed to vote.
Nationality, that is, the Swiss passport.
Adult in the eyes of the law; in Switzerland from 18.

gewusst: In Switzerland over 5 million people are entitled to vote (as of 2024).
In the first vote in 1959, the men still clearly rejected votes for women.
Most voters today vote by post and no longer go to the polling station at all.
