teile.einleitung: The Federal Assembly, that is, the National Council and the Council of States together, works in sessions. These are periods of a few weeks in which parliament sits in Bern. Each session has its fixed routine and its typical business.
wichtigste: The Federal Assembly is a militia parliament and therefore sits in sessions.
In the winter session after the elections, the whole Federal Council is elected.
In the summer session the state accounts are approved.
Tuesday afternoon is set aside for parliamentary group meetings.
On Mondays the National Council only starts at 2.30 pm.
The first session outside Bern took place in Geneva in 1993.

abschnitte.text: Most members of parliament have a **job** alongside their seat. That is why the Federal Assembly is called a **militia parliament**. For this reason it does not meet all year round, but only for a few weeks in **sessions**. In between, the **committees** work. There, smaller groups of members prepare the business.

On **Monday** the National Council only begins at **2.30 pm**, so that members from all over Switzerland can travel there. On the other days it starts at 8 am. **Tuesday afternoon** is kept free: then the **parliamentary groups**, that is, the groups of the parties, hold their discussions. When there is a lot of business, there is an **evening sitting** from 7 pm to 10 pm, usually on the Monday of the second week of the session.

Some business always comes in the same session. The **state accounts** for the previous year show how much money the Confederation took in and spent. They are approved in the **summer session** in June. The **budget** for the next year only comes in winter. After the National Council elections in October, the new legislative period begins with the **winter session**. There, in December, the United Federal Assembly elects the whole **Federal Council**.

Normally parliament sits in the Federal Palace in Bern. But the **autumn session of 1993** took place in **Geneva**, the first session outside Bern. Later, further sessions followed in other parts of the country. In May and June 2020 the chambers met on the **Bernexpo** grounds because of the **COVID-19 pandemic**, because distances could not be kept in the Federal Palace.

gewusst: On Monday the National Council only starts in the afternoon, so that everyone can travel to Bern in time.
The whole Federal Council is always re-elected in December after the National Council elections.

teile.einleitung: The Sonderbund War of 1847 was the last war on Swiss soil. Liberal and Catholic-conservative cantons argued about how Switzerland should be organised. After the war, the modern federal state was created in 1848.
wichtigste: In 1845 seven Catholic-conservative cantons founded the **Sonderbund**.
Inviting the Jesuits to Lucerne made the dispute worse.
On 4 November 1847 the Diet decided to dissolve the Sonderbund by force of arms.
General **Guillaume-Henri Dufour** led the federal troops.
The battle of Gisikon on 23 November 1847 was decisive.
Valais was the last canton to surrender, on 29 November 1847.
The war lasted only a few weeks.

abschnitte.text: In the first half of the 19th century, Switzerland was a loose league of cantons, governed by the Federal Treaty of 1815. The **Liberals** wanted a strong federal state with shared laws. The **Catholic-conservative** cantons feared losing their independence and their faith. When Lucerne invited the **Jesuits** to its higher schools, the Liberals were outraged. This was followed by the Freischaren expeditions, that is, armed marches by volunteers against Lucerne.

On 11 December 1845 seven cantons joined together in Lucerne to form a protective alliance: Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Zug, Fribourg and Valais. Obwalden and Nidwalden were counted together as Unterwalden. The majority of the **Diet**, the assembly of the cantons, saw this as a breach of the Federal Treaty. The Sonderbund cantons hoped for help from **Austria**. But this help never came, because the conservative powers had problems of their own.

On 4 November 1847 the Diet in Bern decided to dissolve the Sonderbund by force of arms. General **Guillaume-Henri Dufour** led the federal troops and tried to avoid casualties as far as possible. The Sonderbund army was under the command of **Johann Ulrich von Salis-Soglio**, a Protestant from the Grisons. On 23 November the decision came at the battle of **Gisikon** on the River Reuss. The following day Lucerne was occupied.

After Lucerne, the other Sonderbund cantons gave up too. **Valais** was the last canton to surrender, on 29 November 1847. So the war lasted just under four weeks. Because Dufour acted quickly and carefully, there were comparatively few deaths. This helped the opponents to make peace again after the war.

After the Liberals' victory, the **Federal Constitution of 1848** was created. The loose confederation of states became a federal state with a Federal Council and a Federal Assembly. But the cantons kept many rights, which is called **federalism**. The Sonderbund War is regarded as the last war in Switzerland. To this day the Dufourspitze, the highest peak in Switzerland, is a reminder of the general.

gewusst: The Dufourspitze in the Monte Rosa massif is named after General Dufour.
The commander-in-chief of the Catholic Sonderbund was himself a Protestant.
Only about half a year after the end of the war, the new Federal Constitution was accepted in 1848.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Trade Union Federation, SGB for short, is the largest umbrella organisation of employees in Switzerland. Many individual trade unions are joined together in it. It campaigns for good wages, good working conditions and secure pensions.
wichtigste: The SGB was founded in 1880.
It represents the interests of employees.
Its largest member union is Unia.
The VPOD organises staff in the public service.
In 2024 the people and the cantons accepted the initiative for a 13th AVS pension.
The minimum wage initiative was clearly rejected in 2014.
The SGB has traditionally been close to the SP.

abschnitte.text: A **trade union** is an association of employees. Together they carry more weight when they negotiate wages and working hours with employers. The SGB is an **umbrella organisation** of such unions. It was founded in **1880**, which makes it one of the oldest umbrella organisations in Switzerland. It represents its members' concerns to politicians and employers.

The largest trade union in Switzerland is **Unia**. It was formed in 2004 mainly from the GBI, the SMUV and the VHTL, that is, from unions for construction, industry and trade. Unia organises workers in construction, industry, trades and private services. The **VPOD** represents employees of the Confederation, the cantons, the municipalities and public companies. The **SEV** union mainly organises transport staff.

abschnitte.titel: Wins and defeats at the ballot box
abschnitte.text: The SGB also launches **popular initiatives**. In May 2014 the minimum wage initiative called for a national minimum wage of 22 francs an hour. About 76 per cent of voters rejected it. On **3 March 2024**, however, the people and the cantons accepted the initiative for a **13th AVS pension**. For an initiative from the trade unions, that was unusual.

Historically, the SGB has been close to **social democracy**. Many of its leading figures sit in the federal parliament for the **SP**. Its counterpart in the social partnership is the employers' associations. The trade unions often negotiate **collective labour agreements** with them, which set out wages and working hours.

gewusst: With the 13th AVS pension, the trade unions won a vote in 2024 that many people had not expected.
Unia was formed in 2004 from several unions and is now the largest in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Classified Compilation of Federal Legislation, SR for short, contains the federal law currently in force. Every law, ordinance and treaty has its own number in it. This way you find rules on the same topic together.
wichtigste: The SR is ordered by subject area.
The Federal Constitution has the number SR 101.
The Civil Code has SR 210, the Code of Obligations SR 220.
The digit 3 at the beginning stands for criminal law.
International treaties begin with a 0.
The SR also contains the cantonal constitutions.
The electronic version is updated continuously.

abschnitte.text: The **Classified Compilation** is a collection of the **federal law** in force. It contains laws, ordinances and **international treaties**. The **cantonal constitutions** are included too. **Court rulings**, on the other hand, are not part of it. Today the SR is found mainly in electronic form on the internet.

The acts are ordered by **subject area**. The first digit shows the area: **1** stands for state, people and authorities, **2** for **private law**, **3** for **criminal law**. **9**, for example, stands for the economy. This way you find rules on one topic together, even if they were made at different times.

The **Federal Constitution** of 18 April 1999 is listed under **SR 101**. Under **SR 210** you find the **Civil Code**. Right after it, under **SR 220**, comes the **Code of Obligations**. If you know these numbers, you can find the most important laws quickly.

Treaties with other states have a **0** placed in front. The **European Convention on Human Rights**, for example, has the number **0.101**. This is how **international law** is told apart from **domestic law**. Within international law, the same order by subject area applies again.

Laws change again and again. That is why the electronic SR is **updated continuously**. So it always shows the **current version**. New acts and changes are first published in the **Official Compilation** and then worked into the SR.

gewusst: The Criminal Code has the number SR 311.0.
The SR exists in German, French and Italian, and important acts also in Romansh and English.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Trade Association, SGV for short, is the umbrella organisation of Switzerland's small and medium-sized enterprises. These include, for example, bakeries, joiners' workshops, hairdressing salons and engineering offices. It was founded in 1879 and has its headquarters in Bern.
wichtigste: The SGV represents small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).
SMEs have fewer than 250 employees.
Over 99 per cent of Swiss companies are SMEs.
The SGV was founded in 1879 and has its headquarters in Bern.
It fights for less bureaucracy and lower regulatory costs.
It is strongly committed to dual vocational training.

abschnitte.text: **SME** stands for small and medium-sized enterprises. According to the Federal Statistical Office, these are companies with fewer than **250 employees**. Larger companies are called large enterprises. Over 99 per cent of all companies in Switzerland are SMEs. The SGV is their **umbrella organisation** and represents their concerns in politics.

The Trade Association was founded in **1879**. This makes it a little older than the Swiss Trade Union Federation. Its headquarters are in **Bern**, near the Federal Palace. So it is close to what happens in politics. Every year it holds the “Trade Winter Conference” in **Klosters**. There, representatives of trade and politicians discuss economic policy.

An important concern of the SGV is **reducing regulatory costs**. Rules and forms are often a bigger burden for small firms than for large ones. After all, a small business has no department of its own to deal with them. The SGV therefore campaigns for less regulation and lower administrative costs.

A large share of apprenticeships are offered by SMEs. That is why **dual vocational training** is very important to the SGV. “Dual” means twofold: you learn at the **training company** and at the **vocational school**. The association also publishes a newspaper, the **Schweizerische Gewerbezeitung**.

gewusst: Almost all companies in Switzerland are SMEs: over 99 per cent.
The Trade Association is a year older than the Swiss Trade Union Federation.

teile.einleitung: UNICEF is the children's fund of the United Nations (UN). All over the world it works to make sure that children grow up healthy, can go to school and are protected.
wichtigste: UNICEF belongs to the UN and helps children in many countries.
UNICEF was founded on 11 December 1946, shortly after the Second World War.
Its headquarters are in New York, where the UN also has its headquarters.
UNICEF relies on voluntary contributions from states and on donations.
In 1965 UNICEF received the Nobel Peace Prize.
The light blue logo shows a mother holding up her child in front of a globe.
UNICEF Switzerland and Liechtenstein is based in Zurich.

abschnitte.text: After the **Second World War**, many children in Europe were hungry, ill or had no home any more. That is why on 11 December 1946 the UN founded an aid organisation for children. At first it was mainly about **emergency aid** with food, milk and clothes. Later UNICEF extended its work to the whole world. Today it helps especially in countries where many children live in poverty.

UNICEF makes sure that children get **vaccinations**. Vaccinations protect against dangerous diseases such as measles. The organisation also brings clean water, food and medicine to emergency areas. It supports schools so that more children learn to read and write. UNICEF also campaigns for **children's rights**, which are set out in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.

UNICEF's logo is **light blue**, like the colour of the United Nations. It shows an adult, usually seen as a mother, holding up a child. Behind them you can see a **globe** with olive branches, as in the UN emblem. The picture means: UNICEF protects children all over the world. You can recognise the logo on aid supplies, posters and appeals for donations.

UNICEF does not get fixed money from the UN budget, but relies on **voluntary contributions**. These come from states, companies and many individual people. In many countries there are national committees that collect donations and provide information. The committee **UNICEF Switzerland and Liechtenstein** is based in Zurich. School classes and children help too, for example with collections or sponsored runs.

gewusst: The name UNICEF comes from “United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund”.
UNICEF is one of the few organisations to have received the Nobel Peace Prize, namely in 1965.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Employers' Association represents employers, that is, companies that hire people. It deals with questions about the labour market, education and social insurance. Its counterpart is the trade unions.
wichtigste: The association was founded in 1908 and has its headquarters in Zurich.
It is an umbrella organisation of industry and regional employers' organisations.
It deals with the labour market, education and social policy.
It represents Swiss employers in the International Labour Organization.
It relies on social partnership with the trade unions.
It usually opposes minimum wages set by law.

abschnitte.text: The Employers' Association is an **umbrella organisation**. Its members are mainly **industry associations**, regional employers' organisations and a few individual companies. Together they represent a large share of the people employed in Switzerland. The association has its headquarters in **Zurich**.

The association was founded in **1908** as the “Central Association of Swiss Employers' Organisations”. It was a reaction to the trade unions, which were growing stronger at the time. It kept this old name until 1996. Today it is called the Swiss Employers' Association.

In Switzerland, employers and trade unions often negotiate wages and working conditions themselves. This is called **social partnership**. The results are usually set out in **collective labour agreements**, GAV for short. The state only steps in to add to them. That is why the Employers' Association usually opposes **minimum wages** set by law. For example, it fought against the minimum wage initiative of 2014. The trade unions see it differently and call for minimum wages.

The **AVS** and the pension fund (**BVG**) are largely funded through contributions from wages. Employers and employees pay these together. That is why the Employers' Association has a strong say in pension reforms. **Vocational training** is also important to it, because companies offer many apprenticeships.

The **International Labour Organization** (ILO) has its headquarters in Geneva. It has a three-part structure: governments, employers and workers work together in it. Swiss employers are represented there by the Employers' Association.

gewusst: In the International Labour Organization in Geneva, states, employers and workers sit at one table.
The Employers' Association was founded because the trade unions were becoming stronger and stronger.

teile.einleitung: After every vote, the votes have to be counted. Only then do you know which proposal has won. For the result to be right, you count carefully, honestly and preferably in pairs.
wichtigste: After a vote, you first count the **votes**.
The person who counts the votes is called a **vote counter**.
Counting in pairs is more accurate, because you check each other.
You sort the papers into **piles** for yes and no.
There must never be more votes than voters.
Every vote is equally important.

abschnitte.text: After a vote, there are lots of papers in the **ballot box**. Only when you have counted them all do you know the result. In votes there are **vote counters** for this. They count every vote carefully and honestly. After all, every vote is equally important.

It is best to make two **piles**: one for yes and one for no. Then you count each pile. Often two children count together so that nobody miscounts. They check each other, so mistakes are noticed quickly. In the municipalities too, several people always count together.

If yes has 9 votes and no has 8 votes, then **9 plus 8 equals 17** children have voted. You compare this number with the number of children in the class. If there are 22 children in the class but only 21 papers in the ballot box, one child did not vote. That is allowed. This is how you can check whether everything adds up.

Each child has only **one vote**. If there are more papers in the ballot box than there are children in the class, something has gone wrong. Someone has put in too many papers. In this case you have to **vote again**. There must never be more votes than voters.

gewusst: In big votes in Switzerland, people count the ballot papers in every municipality.
With a simple addition you can check whether the number of votes is right.

teile.einleitung: Anyone accused of a crime has the right to a defence. A lawyer stands up for the accused person. This makes sure that their rights are respected during the proceedings.
wichtigste: The defence represents only the interests of the accused person.
Accused people may call in a defence lawyer from the very first police interview.
Nobody has to incriminate themselves: you may refuse to give a statement.
If a prison sentence of more than one year is possible, a defence is compulsory.
If there is no money, the state appoints an official defence lawyer.
Lawyers are bound by professional secrecy.

abschnitte.text: A **criminal defence lawyer** stands up for the **accused person** alone. They make sure that the person's rights are respected in the proceedings. This is important, because the **presumption of innocence** applies until there is a verdict. Even someone accused of something serious is entitled to a fair trial.

Nobody has to **incriminate themselves**. Accused people have the right to **refuse to give a statement**. They must be told this at the start of an **interview**. Since the **Criminal Procedure Code of 2011**, the so-called **lawyer of the first hour** has applied. This means the defence may be present at the very first questioning by the police.

Accused people may choose a lawyer they trust. This is called a **chosen defence**, and you usually pay for it yourself. In serious cases a **mandatory defence** is required, for example if a prison sentence of **more than one year** is possible. If there is no money, the authority appoints an **official defence lawyer**. The state pays the costs at first.

Lawyers are bound by **professional secrecy**. They may not pass on what they are told without consent. This means accused people can speak openly with their defence. Even in **pre-trial detention**, the defence may visit their client and talk freely with them without the content being monitored.

gewusst: The person represented by a lawyer is called the client.
The right to a defence is also set out in the Federal Constitution and in the European Convention on Human Rights.

t1y0a4if.t: UN Convention on the Rights of the Child

teile.einleitung: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child is a treaty that sets out the rights of all children. Almost all countries in the world have accepted it, including Switzerland. Every person under 18 counts as a child.
wichtigste: The Convention on the Rights of the Child was adopted by the UN General Assembly.
It has 54 articles.
Children's rights apply to all children.
The best interests of the child must come first in decisions.
Every child has a right to life.
Almost all countries in the world have accepted the Convention.
With the third optional protocol, children can complain to the UN.

abschnitte.text: The **UN General Assembly** adopted the **Convention on the Rights of the Child** in **1989**. Representatives of almost all countries in the world sit in the General Assembly. The Convention has **54 articles**, that is, numbered sections. Almost all countries have accepted it. No other UN human rights treaty has so many members.

Children's rights apply to **all children**, no matter where they come from, what language they speak or how their family lives. Nobody may be put at a disadvantage. According to **Article 3**, the **best interests of the child** must be a primary consideration in all decisions. So you always ask what is good for the child.

**Article 6** says that every child has an inherent **right to life**. States should ensure the child's survival and **development**. Children also have a right to **education**, to **health**, and to play and free time. And they have the right to give their **opinion** when something concerns them.

States must protect children from **violence** and exploitation. They should also prevent children from being **abducted** or sold. Countries work together on this. Children who have done something forbidden must be treated **fairly** and with respect for their **dignity**. In prison they must be kept apart from adults.

**Switzerland** ratified the Convention on the Rights of the Child in **1997**. It has also accepted the **third optional protocol**. This means that children whose rights have been violated can send a communication to the **UN Committee on the Rights of the Child**. But first they have to use up all the **legal remedies** in their own country.

gewusst: Every year on 20 November the international day of children's rights is celebrated, because the Convention was adopted on that day in 1989.
The USA is the only UN member that has not ratified the Convention on the Rights of the Child.

teile.einleitung: A city parliament is the elected assembly of a city. Instead of all voters deciding at a meeting, they elect representatives. Depending on the place, this parliament has very different names.
wichtigste: Large cities have a **parliament** because too many people live there for a municipal assembly.
In Zurich the city parliament is called the **Gemeinderat** and has 125 members.
In Bern it is called the **Stadtrat** and has 80 members.
In some cantons, such as Aargau, it is called the **Einwohnerrat**.
The Zurich city parliament is elected every four years.
Most Swiss municipalities do not have a parliament but a municipal assembly.

abschnitte.text: In small municipalities the voters meet at the **municipal assembly** and decide directly. But in a big city not everyone would fit into one hall. That is why the voters elect a **parliament** that debates and decides for them. In 2023 only about one municipality in five had a parliament, mainly towns and larger municipalities. On important questions the voters can still vote at the ballot box.

In **Zurich** the city parliament is called the **Gemeinderat**. This can be confusing, because in many villages the Gemeinderat is the government. In **Bern** the parliament is called the **Stadtrat**, while in Zurich the Stadtrat is the government. In Aargau, Lucerne and Basel-Landschaft a municipal parliament is often called the **Einwohnerrat**. So if you want to know what is meant, you always have to pay attention to the place.

The Gemeinderat of the city of Zurich has **125 members** and is one of the largest municipal parliaments in Switzerland. The Bern Stadtrat has **80 members** and meets in the town hall in the old town. The members of the Zurich Gemeinderat are elected by the people **every four years**. The election takes place together with the election of the city government. Most members belong to parties and form parliamentary groups.

The city parliament decides on the city's **budget** and accounts. It makes rules for the city and checks the work of the city government. With motions, members can ask questions or put forward new ideas. The meetings are chaired by a **president of the council**. This office usually changes every year.

gewusst: In Zurich the Stadtrat is the government, but in Bern it is the parliament.
The Zurich city parliament has more members than some cantonal parliaments.

teile.einleitung: Traffic rules make sure that everyone can get around safely on the road. If you are out on foot or on a bike, you should know the most important rules.
wichtigste: At the red man you stop; at the green man you may go.
On foot you walk on the pavement.
Never cross the road directly in front of or behind a bus that is standing still.
In Switzerland traffic drives on the right; bikes ride at the right-hand edge.
At the front the bike light shines white, at the back red, and every bike needs a bell.
Before turning, you show the direction with your arm.

abschnitte.text: The **pavement** is made for people on foot. There you are protected from the cars. At the **traffic lights** the rule is: at the **red man** you wait, at the green man you may go. It is best to cross the road at the **zebra crossing**. Beforehand you look left, right and left again.

A **bus** that is standing still blocks the view. Drivers cannot see you, and you cannot see the cars. That is why you never cross the road directly in front of or behind a bus. It is better to wait until the bus has driven off. Then you have a clear view in both directions.

In Switzerland traffic **drives on the right**, so on your bike you ride at the **right-hand edge** of the road. Before **turning**, you stretch out your arm in the direction you want to go. The required equipment includes a **bell** so that you can warn others. At the front a **white light** shines, at the back a **red** one. A cycle helmet is not compulsory for normal bikes, but it protects your head.

abschnitte.titel: Easy to see and well practised
abschnitte.text: Bright clothes, a **high-visibility vest** or reflective strips can be seen from far away. That way drivers notice children better, especially at dusk and in the rain. In many cantons children practise riding their bikes in traffic at school with the **police**. At the end they take the **cycling test**. There they show that they know the rules and ride safely.

gewusst: Since 2021 children under 12 have been allowed to ride their bikes on the pavement if there is no cycle path or cycle lane, but they must be considerate towards pedestrians.
On a zebra crossing in Switzerland, pedestrians have right of way, and cars must stop.

teile.einleitung: Sometimes a vote ends in a tie. Then a rule is needed so that there is still a result. One such rule is the casting vote: a particular person tips the balance.
wichtigste: The **casting vote** helps when there is a tie.
The casting vote is given by one single person.
Who has it is agreed **before the vote**.
In class the **teacher** often has the casting vote.
In the National Council the **president of the chamber** has the casting vote.
After the casting vote the result is fixed.

abschnitte.text: In a vote, the proposal with the most votes normally wins. If both sides have the same number of votes, it is a **tie**. Then a particular person may tip the balance. This is called the **casting vote**. The German word “Stichentscheid” contains “Entscheid” (decision), because it decides something that was open before.

Imagine: 5 children want to go to the zoo, 5 children to the museum. So it is **5 to 5**. If the teacher has the casting vote and chooses the zoo, the class goes to the zoo. It is important to **agree beforehand** who has the casting vote. Then nobody can say the rule was made up specially.

The casting vote always lies with **one single person**. If two people had the casting vote, they could disagree again. Then it would be a tie once more. With one person, on the other hand, there is always a **clear result**. After that it is fixed which proposal has won.

The Swiss parliament also has the casting vote. In the **National Council** the president of the chamber does not normally vote. But if it is a tie, he or she gives the **casting vote**. A rule like this also applies in the Council of States. That way a parliament can always reach a decision, even when there is a deadlock.

gewusst: Whoever presides over the National Council is often called the “highest Swiss woman” or “highest Swiss man”.
In elections, a tie is often decided not by one person but by drawing lots.

teile.einleitung: The number 147 is a counselling service for children and young people in Switzerland. Here you can talk about any worry. The call is free, and you do not have to give your name.
wichtigste: The 147 counselling service is there for children and young people.
It is offered by the Pro Juventute foundation.
A call is free.
You can reach 147 day and night.
You may stay anonymous.
As well as by phone, you can also use text messages and chat.
In an emergency with injured people, you dial 144.

abschnitte.text: The **147 counselling service** is run by the **Pro Juventute** foundation. **Trained professionals** work there; they listen to children and young people and look for solutions with them. The service is specially for children and young people in Switzerland. There are separate services for parents.

A call to 147 is **free of charge**. So anyone can call, even without money. The service can be reached **24 hours** a day, so at night and at weekends too. You can stay **anonymous** and do not have to give your name if you do not want to.

You can **call** 147, send a **text message** or write in the **chat**. Some people find it easier to write than to talk. That way every child finds the way that suits them best. The 147 website also has lots of information on common questions.

At 147 you may talk about **anything**: arguments, fear, heartbreak, problems at home or at school. **No worry is too small**. If you look for help, you are not doing anything wrong. Often it already helps when someone listens and you are not alone.

147 is there for **worries and problems**. In an **emergency** with injured people, you dial **144**, the number for the ambulance and rescue service. You can reach the **police** on **117** and the **fire brigade** on **118**. It is worth knowing these numbers by heart.

gewusst: The number 147 is the same all over Switzerland, on a mobile phone too.
The European emergency number 112 also works in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The voting age tells you how old you have to be to be allowed to vote. In Switzerland it is 18 at federal level. One canton has already lowered it to 16 for its own questions.
wichtigste: At federal level in Switzerland you may vote from the age of 18.
In 2007 the canton of Glarus became the first and so far only canton to introduce a voting age of 16.
In Glarus this only applies to the canton and municipalities, not to federal level.
In Glarus too, you need Swiss citizenship.
In Bern, Zurich and Lucerne voters rejected a voting age of 16.
Austria has allowed voting from 16 since 2007.

abschnitte.text: The **voting age** is the age from which you may take part in votes. At federal level it is **18**. A first attempt to lower it from 20 to 18 was narrowly rejected in **1979**. Only at the second attempt, in **1991**, did the people and the cantons say yes.

In **2007** the canton of **Glarus** decided at the **Landsgemeinde** to introduce a voting age of 16. The Landsgemeinde is an open-air assembly where people vote by raising their hands. Since then 16- and 17-year-olds have been able to take part there too. But for federal votes they have to wait until 18 like everyone else. So the difference is **2 years**.

In Glarus too, the right to vote requires **Swiss citizenship** and residence in the canton. Young people without a Swiss passport may not vote. The voting age is set out in the **cantonal constitution**. That is why a canton's voters have to agree to any change.

There have been votes on a voting age of 16 in several cantons. In **Bern** and **Zurich** voters said no in 2022, in **Lucerne** in 2025. In these cantons the age of 18 still applies. Supporters and opponents have different reasons, and the discussion goes on.

In **Austria**, young people have been able to vote for the national parliament from the age of 16 since 2007. In **Germany**, **France** and **Italy** you vote for the national parliament from 18. Around the world, 18 is the most common voting age.

gewusst: Glarus and Austria introduced a voting age of 16 in the same year, namely 2007.
At the Glarus Landsgemeinde, all voters vote together on the Zaunplatz in Glarus.

teile.einleitung: The United Nations, UN for short, is an organisation in which almost all the states of the world work together. It was founded in 1945 after the Second World War to keep the peace and promote human rights. Switzerland has been a full member since 2002.
wichtigste: The UN was founded in 1945 after the Second World War.
It has 193 member states (as of 2026).
Its headquarters are in New York.
Switzerland has been a full member since 2002.
The Security Council has five permanent members with a right of veto.
The UN has six official languages.
Its predecessor was the League of Nations, based in Geneva.

abschnitte.text: The **United Nations** is an international organisation of states. Its most important aims are peace and security, respect for **human rights** and cooperation between countries. The basic rules are set out in the Charter of the United Nations. With 193 members (as of 2026), almost all the states of the world belong to it.

The UN was founded on 24 October 1945, shortly after the end of the Second World War. At the beginning it had 51 member states. Its predecessor was the **League of Nations**, which was founded in 1920 and had its seat in Geneva. But the League of Nations could not prevent the Second World War and was dissolved in 1946.

In the **General Assembly** each member country has one vote. The **Security Council** is responsible for peace and security and has 15 members. Five of them are permanent: the USA, Russia, China, France and the United Kingdom, and they have a right of veto. The administration is led by the Secretary-General; since 2017 this has been António Guterres from Portugal.

The UN has six official languages: Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish. Many sub-organisations belong to the UN family. The children's fund **UNICEF** works for children, and the World Health Organization (WHO) for health. The World Food Programme helps people who are suffering from hunger.

For a long time Switzerland was only an observer, because many people feared for its **neutrality**. In 1986 the people still clearly rejected joining. On 3 March 2002 the people and the cantons said yes, and in September 2002 Switzerland became the 190th member. In 2023 and 2024 Switzerland sat on the Security Council for the first time as a non-permanent member.

After New York, Geneva is the UN's second most important location. The **Palais des Nations**, the former seat of the League of Nations, now houses the United Nations Office at Geneva. The WHO and many other organisations also have their headquarters in the city. Thousands of international meetings take place there every year.

begriffe.erklaerung: Short for United Nations (in German “UNO”, from United Nations Organization).
The right to block a decision on your own.
The founding treaty that sets out the rules of the UN.
A country does not fight on either side in any war.

gewusst: Switzerland is the only country that joined the UN after a popular vote.
In front of the Palais des Nations in Geneva stands a huge chair with a broken leg, a reminder of the victims of landmines.
24 October is celebrated every year as United Nations Day.

teile.einleitung: A swimming pool is a place where you can swim, play and cool down. In Switzerland people often say “Badi”. Many municipalities have their own Badi or an indoor pool.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the outdoor pool is often called “Badi”.
An indoor pool is under a roof and is open in winter too.
The lifeguard makes sure that nobody drowns.
You shower before swimming.
You do not run at the edge of the pool, because it is slippery.
Children who cannot swim always need someone watching them.

abschnitte.text: An **outdoor pool** is in the open air and is open mainly in summer. In Switzerland it is often called a **Badi**. An **indoor pool** is in a building. That is why you can swim there all year round, even in winter. Many swimming pools belong to the **municipality**. It provides them for the people and for school swimming lessons.

A **lifeguard** works at the swimming pool. They watch the water closely. In an emergency they rescue people and give **first aid**. What they say applies to everyone at the pool. That way swimming stays safe for everyone.

Before swimming you **shower**. That way the water in the pool stays cleaner. You do not run at the **edge of the pool**, because the floor is wet and slippery. If you run, you can fall and hurt yourself. You only jump into the water where it is allowed and deep enough.

In the **non-swimmers' pool** the water is not deep. There children can stand and play safely. **Armbands** help with practising, but they do not replace someone watching. Children who cannot swim always need an adult nearby. At school or on a course, many children learn to **swim** and how to stay safe in the water.

gewusst: The word “Badi” is typically Swiss; in Germany people tend to say “Freibad”.
Armbands help with practising, but they never replace an adult who is keeping watch.

teile.einleitung: In National Council elections, many parties in a canton stand not with just one list but with several. These partial lists of the same party are called sub-lists.
wichtigste: Sub-lists are several electoral lists of the same party in the same canton.
They differ, for example, by gender, party wing, region or age.
Lists for age groups are common, for example from youth parties or senior citizens.
Through a sub-list combination, the votes are added together when the seats are shared out.
In this way a party reaches more voters without losing votes.

abschnitte.text: The National Council is elected in each canton by **proportional representation**. The lists get as many seats as their share of the votes. A party can submit several lists, the **sub-lists**. They differ, for example, by **gender, party wing, region or age**. According to the Federal Statistical Office, almost half of the sub-lists in 2023 were divided by age group, for example as youth or senior lists.

The **Federal Act on Political Rights** allows sub-lists of the same party to be combined with each other. When the seats are shared out, the votes of these lists are first added together. Then the group's seats are shared out among the individual sub-lists. That way no votes are lost if a small sub-list does not win a seat on its own. The votes still go to the party.

Several lists put **more candidates** on the ballot paper. Young voters may feel addressed by a youth party, others by a list from their region. In this way a party appeals to **different groups of voters**. Young candidates can gain experience and become better known on a list of their own. Critics think the many lists make the election confusing.

gewusst: Many candidates under 30 stand in National Council elections on sub-lists of youth parties.

teile.einleitung: A semi-presidential system of government is a mixed form. There is a strong president elected by the people and also a prime minister who needs the confidence of parliament. The best-known example is France.
wichtigste: In a semi-presidential system the president and the prime minister share power.
The president is elected by the people and is independent of parliament.
The prime minister needs a majority in parliament.
France is the classic example, shaped by Charles de Gaulle.
Today the French president is elected for five years.
When the president and the prime minister come from opposing camps, this is called cohabitation.

abschnitte.text: There are different ways of governing a country. In a **presidential system** such as in the USA, the president leads the government alone. In a **parliamentary system**, parliament elects the government. The **semi-presidential system** lies in between. “Semi” means half. Power is divided between the **president** and the **prime minister**. The president is independent of parliament, whereas the prime minister needs its confidence.

The constitution of the **Fifth Republic** of 1958 was shaped by **Charles de Gaulle**. He wanted a strong president and became the first president himself in 1959. The president is elected directly by the **people**. If nobody wins an absolute majority in the first round, there is a **run-off** between the two candidates with the most votes. From 1873 the term of office lasted seven years, the “septennat”. A referendum in 2000 shortened it to **five years** from the 2002 election onwards.

In France the president **appoints** the prime minister. But the prime minister needs a majority in the **National Assembly**, otherwise he or she can be brought down. In turn, the president may **dissolve** the National Assembly and call new elections, at most once a year. Emmanuel Macron did this, for example, in June 2024.

Sometimes a different political camp from the president's wins the parliamentary election. Then the president has to appoint a prime minister from the opposing camp. This is called **cohabitation**, meaning “living together”. It happened, for example, from 1986 to 1988, when President **François Mitterrand** had to govern with Prime Minister **Jacques Chirac**.

The political scientists **Shugart and Carey** distinguish two sub-types. In the **premier-presidential** system, only parliament can dismiss the government. In the **president-parliamentary** system, the president can do so as well. Switzerland has a completely different system: here the seven-member Federal Council governs together, and there is no president with a lot of power.

gewusst: In France it can happen that the president and the prime minister are political opponents and still have to govern together.
The French president used to be elected for seven years.

teile.einleitung: The SRG SSR is the largest media company in Switzerland. It makes radio, television and online content in all four national languages. For this it has a mission from the Confederation, called public service.
wichtigste: SRG stands for Schweizerische Radio- und Fernsehgesellschaft (Swiss Broadcasting Corporation); SSR is the French abbreviation.
The SRG was founded in 1931.
Its headquarters are in Bern.
SRF, RTS, RSI and RTR make programmes for the four language regions.
SWI swissinfo.ch informs people abroad in ten languages.
The SRG SSR is organised as an association.
Since 1 November 2024 Susanne Wille has been Director General (as of 2026).

abschnitte.text: The SRG was founded in February **1931**. It grew out of seven regional **radio companies**. At that time it was only about radio; television was added later. The name **SRG SSR** combines the German and the French abbreviation. The head office is in **Bern**.

The SRG has business units for each language region. **SRF** broadcasts for German-speaking Switzerland, **RTS** for French-speaking Switzerland. **RSI** broadcasts from Ticino for Italian-speaking Switzerland. **RTR** stands for Radiotelevisiun Svizra Rumantscha and makes programmes in Romansh.

The Confederation grants the SRG a **licence**. This sets out its **public service mission**. It is meant to provide all parts of the country and language regions with information, culture, education and entertainment. It is funded mainly by the **radio and television fee**, which households and companies pay.

The SRG SSR is an **association** under the Civil Code. So it is neither a federal office nor a company that wants to make a profit. With **SWI swissinfo.ch** it informs people abroad, especially Swiss people living abroad, in ten languages. Since November 2024 the SRG has been led by **Susanne Wille**; she followed Gilles Marchand.

gewusst: The SRG also makes programmes for Romansh-speaking Switzerland, even though only a small part of the population lives there.
In Switzerland there are repeated political arguments about how high the radio and television fee should be.

teile.einleitung: Vote counters make sure that all votes are counted correctly in votes and elections. In the municipalities they form the electoral office together. Their work is important so that everyone can trust the result.
wichtigste: The vote counters of a municipality form the **electoral office**.
They are usually people from the municipality who are entitled to vote.
Postal votes are first **checked** and then counted.
Vote counters do not reveal how anyone voted (**secrecy of the ballot**).
Invalid ballot papers count neither as yes nor as no.
The municipalities report their results to the **canton**.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, the votes are not counted by machines alone but by people. The **vote counters** are usually quite ordinary residents of the municipality who are entitled to vote. They help out on voting Sunday. Together they form the **electoral office**. It checks and counts all the votes in the municipality.

Many voters vote by post. Their **envelopes** are opened first. Then the **voting card** is checked, so that nobody votes twice. Only after that do the ballot papers go to be counted. This way it stays secret who voted how, and still every valid vote counts.

Vote counters must **keep quiet**. How a particular person voted stays secret. This is called the **secrecy of the ballot**. Results may only be published once voting has closed. That way they do not influence anyone who could still vote.

A ballot paper can be **invalid**, for example if you cannot tell what is meant. Invalid papers are not counted as yes or no. If a result is very close or there are doubts, there is a **recount**. In a recount the votes are counted a second time. This makes it possible to check whether the result is right.

abschnitte.titel: From the village to the canton
abschnitte.text: After counting, each municipality reports its result to the **canton**. The canton adds up all the municipalities. In federal votes, the cantons' results are then added together to make the overall result for Switzerland. At a **municipal assembly**, vote counters have a different task. There they count the raised hands.

gewusst: At municipal assemblies, vote counters count not papers but raised hands.
When results are very close, the votes are counted a second time.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland has been a member of the United Nations (UN) since 10 September 2002. The people and the cantons decided to join in a vote, which was unique in the world.
wichtigste: A first attempt failed in 1986 with 75.7 per cent voting no; all cantons rejected it.
On 3 March 2002, 54.6 per cent of the people said yes; the majority of the cantons was very narrow.
The vote came about through a popular initiative.
Turnout was 58.4 per cent.
Switzerland became the 190th member of the UN.
The Federal Council stressed that Switzerland remains neutral as a member too.
Geneva said yes most clearly, with 66.9 per cent.

abschnitte.text: As early as 1986, Switzerland voted on joining the UN. At that time **75.7 per cent said no**, and not a single canton agreed. Many people felt that joining did not fit with **neutrality**. Switzerland still worked closely with the UN, for example in its specialised agencies. In New York, for a long time it only had observer status.

Citizens collected signatures for the **popular initiative** “for Switzerland's membership of the United Nations Organization”. Because it wanted to change the Federal Constitution, the people and the cantons had to agree. The Federal Council and parliament supported the initiative. The FDP, CVP and SP recommended a yes. The **SVP** and some smaller right-wing parties campaigned against it.

On **3 March 2002**, 58.4 per cent of voters took part. The people said yes with **54.6 per cent**. The majority of the cantons was only reached by a very narrow margin. **Geneva** agreed most clearly, with 66.9 per cent. That is where the UN's European headquarters, the Palais des Nations, stands.

On **10 September 2002** Switzerland was officially admitted as the **190th member**. In its application to join, the Federal Council stated that Switzerland remains neutral. Switzerland was the first country to join because of a **popular vote**. In other countries the government or parliament had decided. As a member, Switzerland can now have its say and vote in the General Assembly.

gewusst: No other country has joined the UN through a popular vote.
Only 16 years passed between the first vote in 1986 and the yes of 2002, but the result turned from three quarters voting no to a yes majority.

teile.einleitung: A State Secretariat is an important federal office with special tasks, often involving cooperation with other countries. It is led by a State Secretary. Each State Secretariat belongs to one of the seven federal departments.
wichtigste: State Secretariats are part of the **Federal Administration** and of a department.
**SECO** is responsible for economic policy and the labour market and belongs to the EAER.
The **SEM** deals with asylum, immigration and naturalisation.
The **SIF** in the Finance Department was created in 2010.
The **SERI** is responsible for education, research and innovation.
Since 2024 the DDPS has had a State Secretariat for Security Policy (**SEPOS**).

abschnitte.text: The Federal Administration is divided into **seven departments**, each led by a member of the Federal Council. Each department has several offices. Some particularly important offices are **State Secretariats**. Their head has the title **State Secretary**. This title helps when Switzerland negotiates abroad with the ministries of other countries.

The Department of Economic Affairs, Education and Research (**EAER**) has two State Secretariats. The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (**SECO**) is the Confederation's centre of expertise for economic policy and the labour market. The State Secretariat for Education, Research and Innovation (**SERI**) is responsible, among other things, for vocational training, universities and funding research. It also looks after cooperation in European research programmes. In Switzerland education and the economy are closely linked, for example in apprenticeships.

The State Secretariat for Migration (**SEM**) belongs to the Federal Department of Justice and Police. At federal level it governs who may enter Switzerland and live here. It carries out **asylum procedures** and is involved in **naturalisation**. For many tasks it works closely with the cantons. The cantons are responsible, for example, for residence permits and accommodation.

The State Secretariat for International Finance (**SIF**) belongs to the Finance Department and was created in 2010. It represents Switzerland's interests in international questions of finance, tax and currency. Since **1979** the Foreign Affairs Department has had a State Secretary as number two after the head of the department, today in the State Secretariat **STS-FDFA**. The newest is the State Secretariat for Security Policy (**SEPOS**) in the DDPS. It started work at the beginning of 2024 and is meant to coordinate the Confederation's security policy strategically.

gewusst: The EAER is the only department with two State Secretariats, SECO and SERI.
The Foreign Affairs Department got its current name in 1979 and a State Secretary at the same time.

teile.einleitung: The United Kingdom does not have a constitution in a single document. Its constitution consists of many laws, court rulings and firm customs that have grown up over centuries.
wichtigste: There is no single constitutional document; people often speak of an unwritten constitution.
Magna Carta of 1215 limited the power of the King.
The Bill of Rights of 1689 strengthened Parliament against the Crown.
A core principle is the sovereignty of Parliament.
Constitutional conventions are unwritten rules that are nevertheless followed.
Since the Human Rights Act of 1998, the ECHR has applied directly in British courts.

abschnitte.titel: Many parts instead of one book
abschnitte.text: Most states have a constitution in a single document, like the Swiss **Federal Constitution**. In the **United Kingdom** it is different. The constitution is made up of **laws**, **court rulings**, conventions and customs. It is often called **unwritten**, even though much of it is written down. It can be changed like an ordinary law, without a popular vote.

abschnitte.titel: Magna Carta and the Bill of Rights
abschnitte.text: **Magna Carta** of 1215 limited the power of King John. To this day it is a symbol of the idea that even the ruler is bound by the law. After the **Glorious Revolution** and the removal of James II, the **Bill of Rights** came about in 1689. It made the Crown dependent on Parliament's consent in important matters. Both documents are among the foundations of the British constitution.

A core principle is **parliamentary sovereignty**. Parliament can make or repeal any law. No court can declare an Act of Parliament invalid. The lawyer **A. V. Dicey** also described how no Parliament can bind its successors. Since the **Human Rights Act** of 1998, people have been able to rely directly on the European Convention on Human Rights in British courts, but the courts only make a declaration of incompatibility.

Many rules are not written in any law. These **constitutional conventions** are politically binding but cannot be enforced in court. For example, the monarch acts on the advice of the government. The monarch also signs every law; this is called **Royal Assent**. The last time it was refused was by **Queen Anne** in **1708**, and never since.

gewusst: Apart from the United Kingdom, only very few states have no constitution in a single document, such as New Zealand and Israel.
Of Magna Carta of 1215, only a few sentences are still in force as law today.

teile.einleitung: Arguments are part of life, but they can be settled fairly. In conflict resolution, a neutral person helps the people who are arguing to find a solution themselves. Many schools have specially trained children for this.
wichtigste: Peer mediators help others to settle an argument.
They are neutral and do not take sides.
In the conversation you let each other finish speaking.
With I-messages you say how you feel.
Hitting is never allowed in an argument.
A solution that both sides are happy with is called an agreement.

abschnitte.text: At many schools **peer mediators** are specially trained. They help when two children are having an argument. They do not hand out a solution but help the people arguing to find one **themselves**. A good mediator is **neutral**. They do not take sides, so that both can trust them.

In conflict resolution there are clear **rules**. Each side may tell their story without being **interrupted**. You listen to each other and do not insult anyone. That way both feel taken seriously. If you feel understood, you are more likely to meet the other person halfway.

With an **I-message** you say how you feel. For example: “I'm sad because you laughed at me.” This way you do not attack the other person. Sentences like “You're always mean”, on the other hand, often make an argument worse. I-messages help both sides to stay calm.

When you are very **angry**, it helps to **take a deep breath**. That calms the body. Afterwards you can talk better. **Violence** does not settle an argument; it makes it worse and it hurts. You may argue, but only with words.

In the end you look for an **agreement** that both sides are happy with. Because both get something out of it, a solution like this usually lasts a long time. Often you **shake hands** at the end. If it does not work on your own, you may ask a **teacher** for help. Getting help is the right thing to do.

gewusst: Among adults, conflict resolution is often called mediation.
In many cantons there are justices of the peace who mediate in disputes between adults.

teile.einleitung: The city president is at the head of a Swiss city. He or she leads the city government and represents the city to the outside world. In everyday speech people often say “Stapi”.
wichtigste: A Swiss city is led by the **city president**.
In Zurich the city government is called the **Stadtrat** and has nine members.
**Corine Mauch** became the first woman city president of Zurich in 2009.
In Bern the government is called the **Gemeinderat** and has five members.
**Marieke Kruit** has been the first woman city president of Bern since 2025.
In Geneva the office of **Maire** changes every year.

abschnitte.text: The **city president** is a member of the city government and chairs its meetings. The government decides together; this is called the **collegial principle**. The city president represents the city at events, on visits and in the media. In addition, he or she usually also runs a department. In German-speaking Switzerland the city president is usually elected directly by the people.

In the city of Zurich the government is called the **Stadtrat**. It consists of **nine members**, and each one leads a department of the city. The city president chairs the meetings of the Stadtrat. In 2009 **Corine Mauch** became the first woman city president of Zurich. She stayed in office for many years.

In the city of Bern the government is called the **Gemeinderat**. It has only **five members**. The city president is one of them and leads it. **Marieke Kruit** was elected at the end of 2024 and took office on 1 January 2025. She is the first woman at the head of the federal city.

In **Geneva** there is no fixed city president. There, a different member of the city government takes on the office of **Maire** every year. In French-speaking Switzerland and in Ticino the office is often called “Syndic” or “Sindaco”. In **Germany** and **Austria** the head of a city is called the **Bürgermeister** (mayor). In German-speaking Switzerland, however, people usually say city president.

gewusst: The word “Stapi” is short for “Stadtpräsident”, the German word for city president.
Bern only had a woman as city president from 2025, Zurich since 2009.

teile.einleitung: The power to tax is the right to collect taxes. In Switzerland the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities share this power. Each level may only collect certain taxes, and the cantons have a lot of freedom.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the **Confederation**, the **cantons** and the **municipalities** have the power to tax.
Only the Confederation may collect **VAT**.
**Wealth tax** is collected only by the cantons and municipalities.
**Inheritance tax** is a matter for the cantons.
The **Tax Harmonisation Act** makes the rules uniform, not the tax rates.
If you move, you pay income tax in the canton where you live at the end of the year.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland is a **federal** state with the Confederation, cantons and municipalities. All three levels may collect taxes. But the **Confederation** may only collect the taxes that the **Federal Constitution** expressly allows it. The **cantons** may collect all other taxes. The **municipalities** may collect taxes as far as the canton allows them to.

According to the Federal Constitution, **VAT** is a federal tax. The cantons may not collect a tax of the same kind. On top of that come the direct federal tax on income and profit, customs duties and the mineral oil tax. The Confederation does not collect a tax on the wealth of private individuals. The Confederation may only collect VAT and the direct federal tax for a limited time; the people must extend them again and again.

abschnitte.titel: Taxes of the cantons and municipalities
abschnitte.text: **Wealth tax** is a matter for the cantons and municipalities. Each canton also governs **inheritance tax** itself; there is no federal inheritance tax. Anyone who sells a piece of land at a profit pays the **property gains tax** to the canton and in some cases the municipality. Companies pay **profit tax** on their profits to the Confederation, the canton and the municipality. The cantons set their own tax rates for this.

Because each canton sets its own tax rates, some cantons try to attract companies and residents with low taxes. This is called **tax competition**. So that not everything is different, there is the **Tax Harmonisation Act**. It sets out what is taxed and how the procedure works. But the cantons still decide how high the taxes are.

What happens if someone moves to another canton during the year? What counts is where you live at the end of the tax period, that is, on **31 December**. That canton taxes the whole year's income. So you do not have to pay taxes to two cantons at once. In fact, the Federal Constitution forbids **double taxation** between cantons.

gewusst: For its most important taxes, the Confederation needs the approval of the people and the cantons again and again.
In Switzerland there is no federal inheritance tax, only cantonal ones.

teile.einleitung: The Council of States is one of the two chambers of the Swiss parliament. It represents the cantons and has 46 members. Together with the National Council it forms the Federal Assembly, which passes laws.
wichtigste: The Council of States is the smaller chamber of the Swiss parliament.
It has 46 members.
20 cantons send two members each, six cantons one member each.
The Council of States and the National Council have equal rights.
The members are elected every four years.
The Council of States sits in the Federal Palace in Bern.
A law needs the approval of both chambers.

abschnitte.titel: What is the Council of States?
abschnitte.text: The Swiss parliament is called the **Federal Assembly** and consists of two chambers. The National Council with 200 members represents the people. The **Council of States** represents the cantons, which used to be called Stände. It is also called the smaller chamber.

Each of the 20 cantons with a whole cantonal vote elects two members to the Council of States. The six cantons of Obwalden, Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden elect one each. That makes 46 members. So large and small cantons are represented almost equally, no matter how many people live there.

The members of the Council of States are elected every four years by the people of their canton. Each canton decides for itself how the election works. Usually the **majority system** applies, which means that whoever has the most votes is elected. Only the cantons of Jura and Neuchâtel elect by proportional representation.

The Council of States and the National Council have exactly the same rights; this is called a **bicameral system**. Every law must be accepted by both chambers with the same wording. If they do not agree, there is a procedure to resolve the differences. For elections, such as that of the Federal Council, both chambers meet as the United Federal Assembly.

The Council of States has existed since the federal state was founded in 1848. Its model was the US Senate, in which each state has two seats. In this way the founders found a compromise between large and small cantons. Debates in the Council of States are often calmer and more factual than in the larger National Council.

The Council of States sits in the **Council of States chamber** in the Federal Palace in Bern. It meets four times a year for a three-week session. It is chaired by the President of the Council of States, who changes every year. Anyone who wants to say something in the debate speaks from their seat.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part of a parliament that debates and votes on its own.
A parliament with two parts that have equal rights.
A voting method in which whoever has the most votes wins.
The Swiss parliament, made up of the National Council and the Council of States.

gewusst: The canton of Zurich has as many members of the Council of States as the much smaller canton of Uri, namely two.
There is no speaker's lectern in the Council of States chamber; members speak from their seats.
If the votes are tied in the Council of States, the president decides with the casting vote.

teile.einleitung: The suffragettes were women in Great Britain who fought for women's right to vote at the beginning of the 20th century. They drew attention to their cause with eye-catching actions. Their name comes from the English word “suffrage”.
wichtigste: “Suffrage” means the right to vote.
Emmeline Pankhurst founded the Women's Social and Political Union in Manchester in 1903.
The motto was “Deeds, not words”.
Many imprisoned suffragettes went on hunger strike.
Their colours were purple, white and green.
Since 1928 women in Great Britain have had the same right to vote as men.

abschnitte.text: The English word **“suffrage”** means the **right to vote**. The **suffragettes** fought for women to be allowed to vote. At that time only men could vote for parliament in Great Britain. Many women thought this was unfair and wanted to change it.

**Emmeline Pankhurst** founded the **Women's Social and Political Union** in **Manchester** in **1903**, together with her daughters. The motto was **“Deeds, not words”**. The suffragettes wanted to stand out with actions instead of just asking. They organised demonstrations, disrupted meetings and sometimes also damaged property.

Many suffragettes were **arrested** for their actions. In prison they often protested with a **hunger strike**, which means they refused to eat. The authorities then often fed them by force. In 1913 **Emily Wilding Davison** ran onto the track at the horse race in **Epsom**. She was struck by the King's horse and died a few days later.

As a sign of recognition, the suffragettes wore **purple, white and green**. Purple stood for dignity, white for purity and green for hope. Other campaigners for women's rights relied only on peaceful means such as **petitions** and talks. They were called **suffragists**, and their best-known representative was **Millicent Fawcett**.

In **1918**, at first only women aged 30 and over who met certain conditions were allowed to vote. From **1928** the same voting age of **21** applied to women and men. In **Switzerland** it took much longer: women only got the vote at federal level in **1971**.

gewusst: The word “suffragette” was first a mocking name used by a newspaper, which the women then proudly took over.
Appenzell Innerrhoden was the last canton, in 1990, to have to introduce votes for women after a ruling by the Federal Supreme Court.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Psalm is the national anthem of Switzerland. A national anthem is a solemn song that stands for a whole country. People sing the Swiss Psalm on 1 August and hear it before international matches.
wichtigste: The tune was written by the monk Alberich Zwyssig in 1841.
The German text was written by Leonhard Widmer from Zurich.
In 1961 the Swiss Psalm became the anthem on a provisional basis.
Since 1981 it has officially been the national anthem.
In French it begins with “Sur nos monts, quand le soleil”.
In the past “Rufst du, mein Vaterland” was the anthem.

abschnitte.text: **Alberich Zwyssig** was a **monk** at Wettingen Abbey. He was also a musician and composer. **Leonhard Widmer** from Zurich wrote a text and gave it to Zwyssig, who set it to music in **1841**. This is how the Swiss Psalm came about. A **psalm** is a solemn, religious song.

Before the Swiss Psalm became the anthem, people sang “**Rufst du, mein Vaterland**” for a long time. But this song had the same tune as the English anthem. When both countries met at an event, this often led to mix-ups. That is why a separate anthem was looked for.

abschnitte.titel: The road to the official anthem
abschnitte.text: In **1961** the Federal Council first declared the Swiss Psalm the anthem only **provisionally**. Provisionally means for the time being, on trial. Only in **1981** did it finally become the official national anthem. So twenty years passed in between.

The Swiss Psalm exists in all the **national languages**. In French it begins with “Sur nos monts, quand le soleil”. Do not mix it up: “Allons enfants de la patrie” is the beginning of the French anthem, the Marseillaise. On **1 August** the Swiss Psalm is sung at many celebrations, and it is also played before international matches.

gewusst: The former Swiss anthem had the same tune as the English anthem.
For twenty years the Swiss Psalm was only an anthem on trial.

teile.einleitung: For many people, social media such as Instagram, TikTok, YouTube or X are part of everyday life. They also play a big role in politics, for example before elections and votes. If you want to use them wisely, you should know their opportunities and dangers.
wichtigste: Parties and committees use social media for their campaigns.
In Switzerland political advertising on radio and television is banned.
With **microtargeting**, small groups receive advertising tailored to them.
In a **filter bubble** you mainly see content that matches your own opinion.
In an **echo chamber** like-minded people confirm each other's views.
**Social bots** are programs that post like humans.
Paid posts are labelled “Sponsored” or “Ad”.

abschnitte.text: On social media anyone can publish, comment on and share posts. That is why parties, politicians and referendum committees also use these platforms. In Switzerland the **Radio and Television Act** bans political advertising on radio and television. Campaigns therefore turn to posters, newspaper adverts and social media. With **hashtags** such as #vote, posts are linked to a topic and are easier to find.

Platforms collect a lot of data about what their users like. With **microtargeting**, this data is used to tailor political advertising precisely to small groups. This means that different people see completely different messages. Paid posts must be labelled with notes such as “Sponsored” or “Ad”. That way you can tell that someone has paid for them to be spread.

Platforms often show posts that match what you have already watched or liked. This can create a **filter bubble**, in which other points of view appear less often. In an **echo chamber**, mainly like-minded people are among themselves. You hear your own opinion come back from others like an echo, and there is hardly any disagreement. In this way opinions can become stronger without you noticing.

Not every account has a person behind it. **Social bots** are programs that automatically write, share or like posts. They can make an opinion seem bigger than it really is. **Influencers** are people with many followers who can shape opinions with their reach. That is why they are sometimes used in election campaigns too.

With political posts it is worth asking: who wrote this, and where does the information come from? Reliable media and official bodies such as the Confederation help to check claims. If you deliberately follow other opinions too, you find it easier to get out of the filter bubble. Before sharing, you should think briefly about whether a message is true. That way everyone helps to keep debates fair.

gewusst: The internet activist Eli Pariser made the term “filter bubble” well known with a book in 2011.
The ban on political advertising on radio and television is a Swiss peculiarity that does not exist in this form in many other countries.

teile.einleitung: Taking responsibility means looking after something and standing by it, even when something goes wrong. This applies to yourself, to other people, to animals and to the environment.
wichtigste: Anyone who takes responsibility looks after a task and stands by it.
You admit mistakes, apologise and help to put them right.
The owners are responsible for a pet.
Taking your rubbish with you means taking responsibility for the environment.
In traffic you are responsible for yourself and for others.
Article 6 of the Federal Constitution speaks of every person's responsibility.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who takes **responsibility** looks after a task reliably. You can **rely** on this person. In class this shows, for example, when a child does their **class job** (in Swiss German an “Ämtli”) well. Responsibility also means standing by your own actions. This applies when something goes well, but also when something goes wrong.

Everyone makes mistakes. If you have broken something by accident, you **admit it** and **apologise**. Then you help to make up for the damage. You are also responsible for others. If a younger child falls over in the playground, you help and fetch a **teacher**.

A **pet** needs food, water and care every day. Its **owners** are responsible for this. Everyone can also do something for the **environment**. At a picnic you take your **rubbish** with you or put it in the bin. That way meadows and woods stay clean.

The **Federal Constitution** has a section of its own on this in **Article 6**. It is called “Individual and social responsibility”. Every person should look after themselves and help with the **common good** as far as they can. You also have responsibility in **traffic**: anyone who rides a bike keeps to the rules. That way you protect yourself and others.

gewusst: Many adults take on responsibility voluntarily, for example as a leader in a club or in the fire brigade.
The Federal Constitution begins with rights, but in Article 6 it also reminds us that every person is responsible for the community.

te4tsla.t: Number of signatures for a referendum

teile.einleitung: With a referendum the people can vote on a new federal law. This needs 50,000 valid signatures, which must be collected within 100 days.
wichtigste: An optional referendum needs 50,000 valid signatures.
The time limit is 100 days from the publication of the law in the Federal Gazette.
On average that is 500 signatures a day.
A popular initiative needs twice as many signatures, 100,000.
The Federal Chancellery checks whether there are enough valid signatures.
Eight cantons together can also call for a referendum.

abschnitte.text: If parliament passes a new **federal law**, the people can call a **referendum** against it. This needs **50,000 valid signatures**. That is exactly half of 100,000. If a committee has, for example, 60,000 valid signatures, it is enough. With 45,000, on the other hand, 5000 are still missing.

The time limit starts when the law is published in the **Federal Gazette**. From then on you have **100 days**, that is, just over three months. If you work out 50,000 divided by 100, you get **500 signatures a day**. That is why you have to collect quickly for a referendum. With a popular initiative you have much longer, 18 months.

A **popular initiative** needs **100,000** signatures, so twice as many. It proposes something new and wants to change the Federal Constitution. The referendum, on the other hand, is directed against a law that has already been passed. That is why the time limit is shorter. The people should be able to say quickly whether they want the law.

First the municipalities confirm that the people who signed are entitled to vote. Then the signatures go to the **Federal Chancellery**. It checks whether there are enough valid ones. If the referendum has **succeeded**, there is a popular vote. For a law, a majority of the people is then enough; the majority of the cantons is not needed.

gewusst: Instead of 50,000 voters, eight cantons together can also call for a referendum.
For changes to the Federal Constitution no signatures are needed at all: the people and the cantons always vote on them; this is the mandatory referendum.

teile.einleitung: With a cantonal initiative, a canton can ask the Confederation for a new law or a change to the Federal Constitution. So it is a kind of proposal from a canton to the federal parliament. In this way the cantons can bring their concerns directly to Bern.
wichtigste: A cantonal initiative is a proposal from a canton to the Confederation.
With it a canton calls for a new law or a change to the constitution.
Each of the 26 cantons may submit a cantonal initiative.
It is debated by both chambers of parliament.
Parliament decides whether to take the initiative forward.
The people do not vote directly on a cantonal initiative.

abschnitte.text: The cantons used to be called **Stände**, which is where the German name “Standesinitiative” comes from. With it, a canton can make a proposal to the Federal Assembly. It can call for a new federal law, a change to a law or a change to the Federal Constitution. The right is set out in the **Federal Constitution**.

Each canton decides for itself who in the canton decides on the cantonal initiative. Usually it is the **cantonal parliament**, often on the proposal of one of its members. In some cantons the people can also call for a cantonal initiative. It is then submitted in Bern in the name of the canton.

The cantonal initiative first goes to a **committee** of the National Council or the Council of States. Then both chambers decide whether to **take it forward**. If both say yes, a committee works out a draft law. If one chamber says no twice, the cantonal initiative is finished.

abschnitte.titel: The difference from a popular initiative
abschnitte.text: With a **popular initiative**, citizens collect signatures, and in the end the people vote. With a cantonal initiative, on the other hand, only parliament decides. It is therefore more of a suggestion than an obligation. Many cantonal initiatives are rejected, but some are still put into practice in another way.

With cantonal initiatives, cantons draw attention to problems they cannot solve themselves. Common topics are transport, health, farming, energy or taxes.
