Several cantons often submit similar initiatives to build up more pressure. In this way the cantonal initiative shows Switzerland's **federalism**.

begriffe.erklaerung: An old word for canton.
Parliament says yes to working further on the concern.
The parliament of a canton, often called the Grand Council or Cantonal Council.
The Confederation and the cantons share power.

gewusst: In Switzerland, several dozen cantonal initiatives are often submitted each year.
A cantonal initiative does not have to be fully worded; a general proposal is enough.

teile.einleitung: Public service means basic provision: important services should be available to all people in all regions of Switzerland in good quality and at fair prices. These include, for example, the post, public transport, radio and television, electricity and water.
wichtigste: Public service means basic provision for all regions.
The federal post has existed since 1849.
In 1998 the PTT was split into Swiss Post and Swisscom.
Swiss Post has a remaining monopoly on letters up to 50 grams.
The SBB came about after a popular vote in 1898.
The SBB belongs entirely to the Confederation.
In 1982 the SBB introduced the regular-interval timetable.

abschnitte.text: **Public service** is meant to make sure that it is not only towns that are well served. A mountain village should also receive post, be reachable by bus and have electricity. That is why people speak of **basic provision**. Many of these services are provided by companies that belong wholly or partly to the Confederation, the cantons or the municipalities.

Shortly after the federal state was founded, the Confederation took over the postal service from the cantons on **1 January 1849**. Later the **PTT** came about, which stood for post, telephone, telegraph. In **1998** it was split up: the postal services went to **Swiss Post**, telecommunications to **Swisscom**. In 2025 Swiss Post has a **remaining monopoly** on domestic letters up to 50 grams. With this it funds part of the basic provision.

The **Postal Ordinance** sets out how close a post office must be. 90 per cent of the permanent resident population must be able to reach a post office or a **postal agency** within **20 minutes**, on foot or by public transport. A postal agency is, for example, a counter in a village shop.

In the past, the big railways belonged to private companies. On **20 February 1898** the people agreed that the Confederation should buy them. From **1902** the **SBB** began operating. Since 1999 it has been a public limited company whose shares all belong to the Confederation. In **1982** the SBB introduced the **regular-interval timetable**. Since then trains leave, for example, at the same minute every hour. This makes connections easier and train travel easy to plan.

gewusst: Thanks to the regular-interval timetable of 1982, many trains in Switzerland leave at the same minute every hour.
The people decided at the ballot box in 1898 that Switzerland should have a state railway.

teile.einleitung: The Social Democratic Party of Switzerland, SP for short, is one of the country's big parties. It belongs to the political left and is particularly committed to social justice. It has been represented on the Federal Council for many decades.
wichtigste: The SP was founded in **1888** and belongs to the labour movement.
Its party colour is **red**.
In French it is called **Parti socialiste suisse** (PS).
**Ernst Nobs** was elected to the Federal Council in 1943 as the first Social Democrat.
**Ruth Dreifuss** became the first SP woman on the Federal Council in 1993.
Since 2020 Mattea Meyer and Cédric Wermuth have led the party as co-presidents.

abschnitte.text: The SP grew out of the **labour movement** in the 19th century. At that time many people worked in factories for low wages and in hard conditions. The party wanted to improve their situation, together with the **trade unions**. Since the 19th century red has been the colour of the labour movement and therefore also the colour of the SP. In French-speaking Switzerland the party is called Parti socialiste suisse, PS for short.

In November 1918 the SP and the Swiss Trade Union Federation organised the **general strike**. Many workers stopped working. Among other things, they demanded a 48-hour week, votes for women and old-age insurance. The Federal Council called in the army, and the strike was called off after a few days. But many of the demands were put into practice later, for example with the **AVS**, which was introduced in 1948.

For a long time the SP was not represented in the national government. In 1943 **Ernst Nobs** from Zurich was elected to the Federal Council as the first Social Democrat; he was in office from 1944 to 1951. Since the **magic formula** of 1959 the SP has had two seats on the Federal Council. In 1993 **Ruth Dreifuss** was elected as the party's first woman. In 2025 **Elisabeth Baume-Schneider** and **Beat Jans** represent the party on the Federal Council.

The SP campaigns for a strong welfare state, for equality and for environmental protection. In 2024 its **premium relief initiative** came to the vote. It wanted to limit health insurance premiums to at most 10 per cent of income and was rejected. In its party programme of 2010 the SP comes out in favour of **Switzerland joining the EU**. In this it differs from the centre-right governing parties, which are against joining.

From 2008 to 2020 **Christian Levrat** from Fribourg was president of the SP. In October 2020 a **co-presidency**, that is, a joint leadership, took over. Since then **Mattea Meyer** and **Cédric Wermuth** have led the party together. The SP has its own cantonal parties in all cantons. Like the other parties, it is supported by its members.

gewusst: Since 1959 the SP has had two seats on the Federal Council without a break.
Many demands of the 1918 general strike, such as votes for women, only became reality decades later.

teile.einleitung: The voting age of 16 is about whether 16-year-olds should already be allowed to vote and elect. In Switzerland only the canton of Glarus has this rule. It is also being discussed in other countries.
wichtigste: The cantons set their own rules on political rights for cantonal and municipal questions.
Glarus narrowly introduced a voting age of 16 at the Landsgemeinde in 2007.
In Glarus it applies to the canton and the municipalities.
Several cantons rejected a voting age of 16 at the ballot box.
Austria has voted from 16 nationwide since 2007.
Supporters and opponents have different arguments.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Constitution** leaves it to the cantons to set the rules for votes and elections on **cantonal and municipal** matters. That is why a canton can have a lower voting age than the Confederation. For federal votes, however, **18** applies everywhere.

In 2007 the **Glarus Landsgemeinde** voted **narrowly** for a voting age of 16. At the same time there were even proposals to raise the age to 20. Since then young people aged 16 and over have been able to have a say in the canton and also at **municipal assemblies**. So far Glarus is the only canton with this rule.

In several cantons voters said **no**. Basel-Stadt rejected it in 2009 with 72 per cent, and **Basel-Landschaft** in 2018 with as much as **84.5 per cent**. Neuchâtel said no in 2020 with 58.5 per cent. In 2022 **Zurich** rejected it with about 64 per cent and Bern with 67 per cent.

In 2007 **Austria** introduced a voting age of 16 for all national elections. In **Germany**, 16-year-olds were allowed to vote for the first time in the **2024 European elections**; for the Bundestag election the age is still 18. In **Scotland**, 16- and 17-year-olds already voted in the **independence referendum** of 2014. In **Brazil**, young people may vote voluntarily from 16; from 18 voting is compulsory there.

**Supporters** say that young people are affected by many decisions for a long time. They should therefore have a say earlier on questions that concern their future. **Opponents** think that the right to vote and **coming of age** should be at the same age. In Switzerland you come of age at 18.

gewusst: In the Scottish vote of 2014, the majority voted against independence from Great Britain.
In Glarus 16-year-olds may vote, but they can only be elected to cantonal offices at 18.

teile.einleitung: The voting card shows that someone is allowed to take part in a vote or an election. The municipality sends it home together with the voting papers. Without it you cannot vote.
wichtigste: The municipality sends the voting card home by post.
It arrives a few weeks before voting day together with the papers.
When voting by post, you have to sign it in most cantons.
The ballot paper goes into a small voting envelope.
At the polling station you show your voting card.
The voting booklet explains the proposals.

abschnitte.text: The **municipality** knows who lives there and is allowed to vote. That is why it sends the **voting papers** to all voters. This happens a few weeks before voting day. When you turn 18, you receive your own papers for the first time before the next federal vote.

In the envelope there are the **voting card**, the **ballot papers** and a small **voting envelope**. There is also the **voting booklet**. In it the Federal Council explains the proposals, and the opinions of supporters and opponents are set out too. That way everyone can prepare in peace.

With **postal voting**, you fill in the ballot paper at home and put it in the voting envelope. You seal the envelope so that your vote stays **secret**. In most cantons you have to **sign** the voting card. With your signature you confirm that you voted yourself. Then you send everything back by post or put it in the municipality's letterbox.

If you prefer to vote in person, you take your voting card with you to the **polling station** on voting Sunday. There you show it. That way the helpers can see that you are entitled to vote. Then you put your ballot paper in the sealed **ballot box**. That is why this is called a **ballot box vote**.

gewusst: Most people in Switzerland now vote by post.
In many cantons a postal vote does not count without a signature on the voting card.

teile.einleitung: Turnout shows how many voters took part in a vote or an election. It is given as a percentage. In Switzerland it is important because the people vote very often.
wichtigste: **Turnout** shows the share of voters who voted.
It is given as a **percentage**.
If 40 out of 100 vote, it is 40 per cent.
In Switzerland about **half** or slightly fewer often vote.
Voting is **voluntary** in almost all cantons.
On topics that move many people, turnout is higher.

abschnitte.text: **Turnout** shows what share of the voters took part in a vote. It is given as a **percentage**. For example, if 40 out of 100 voters vote, turnout is 40 per cent. At 50 per cent, **half** have voted, that is, every second person. Whether someone votes yes or no does not matter for this.

You divide the number of people who voted by the number of all voters. Then you multiply by 100. If 600 out of 1200 voters in a municipality vote, that gives 600 divided by 1200 equals 0.5, so 50 per cent. Every person who votes raises turnout. But a high turnout says nothing about which side wins.

In Switzerland voting is **voluntary** in almost all cantons. Only the canton of **Schaffhausen** has a duty to vote. Anyone there who does not vote without a good reason has to pay a small amount. That is why turnout in Schaffhausen is usually higher than in other cantons. Swiss citizens aged 18 and over are entitled to vote; in the canton of Glarus, on cantonal questions, from 16.

In many votes, about **half** of the voters or slightly fewer take part. On topics that are talked about a lot, more people go to vote. A well-known example is the vote on the **European Economic Area** (EEA) in December 1992. At that time almost 80 per cent of voters voted. Because Switzerland votes several times a year, many people do not take part in every vote.

gewusst: In the EEA vote of 1992, almost four out of five voters voted.
Schaffhausen is the only canton with a duty to vote.

teile.einleitung: A tally chart is a simple way of counting. For each vote you draw a line. In class, for example, it helps when you vote on something.
wichtigste: On a tally chart you draw one line for each vote.
You draw four lines next to each other, and the fifth goes across them.
This makes a bundle of five.
With bundles of five you can count faster.
In class the tally chart is often on the blackboard.
At the end you count the lines and compare.

abschnitte.text: On a **tally chart** each vote gets exactly **one line**. That way the number of lines matches the votes. For example, you write “Yes” and “No” and draw the matching lines after each word. At the end you count up.

You draw **four lines** next to each other. You draw the **fifth line** across them. This makes a **bundle of five**. Lots of single lines are hard to count. In bundles of five it is much faster, because you simply count in fives.

Two bundles of five are 5 plus 5, so **10** votes. Three bundles and two single lines are 3 times 5 equals 15, plus 2 makes **17**. If there are only three lines so far, **two** more are needed for the first bundle. If “Yes” has four lines and “No” has a bundle of five, **No** wins, because 5 is more than 4.

In class the tally chart is often written on the **blackboard**. That way all the children can see the lines and **count along**. This makes the vote fair and easy to follow. A tally chart is also handy in games, for counting cars or in surveys.

gewusst: Tally charts are among the oldest ways that humans have counted.
In some countries, such as China, bundles of five are drawn differently, namely with the five strokes of a written character.

teile.einleitung: Taxes are money that people and companies pay to the state. They fund tasks that benefit everyone, for example schools, roads and the police. In Switzerland the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities collect taxes.
wichtigste: With **taxes**, everyone together pays for shared tasks.
**VAT** is included in the price of many goods; children pay it too when they go shopping.
Since 2024 the standard rate of VAT has been **8.1 per cent**.
Since 2024 a lower rate of **2.6 per cent** has applied to food and books.
Anyone who keeps a dog pays a **dog tax**.
**Tax evasion** is forbidden and is punished.

abschnitte.text: Many things in everyday life belong to everyone together. These include **schools**, **roads**, the **police**, hospitals and parks. For the state to be able to carry out these tasks, it needs money. A large part of this money comes from **taxes**. In Switzerland the Confederation, the 26 cantons and the municipalities collect taxes.

**Value added tax** (VAT) is already included in the price of many goods and services. That is why everyone who shops pays it, even a child buying an ice cream. Since 2024 the standard rate has been **8.1 per cent**. For important things such as food and books, a reduced rate of **2.6 per cent** applies. VAT is one of the Confederation's most important sources of income.

Anyone who works and earns money pays **income tax**. For this, adults fill in a **tax return** every year. In it they state how much they have earned and what they own. Anyone who earns more usually pays a higher share. Companies pay taxes too, namely on their profits.

There are also taxes on very specific things. Anyone who keeps a dog pays a **dog tax**, which usually goes to the municipality. When you fill up with fuel, the price of petrol and diesel includes the Confederation's **mineral oil tax**. Part of it is used for roads. The Confederation also charges special taxes on tobacco and alcohol.

Paying taxes is a duty. Anyone who deliberately hides income or assets commits **tax evasion**. This is forbidden and is punished with a fine. In Switzerland voters often have a say in how high taxes are. That way the people can help decide how much money the state spends on which tasks.

gewusst: In Switzerland the people can vote on taxes, which is not possible in many countries.
Even when you buy an ice cream you pay VAT, at the lower rate for food.

teile.einleitung: A social bot is a computer program that runs an account on social networks and pretends to be a human. Such bots can spread opinions and make topics seem bigger than they are. That is why it is important for democracy to recognise them.
wichtigste: Social bots are programs that post, share and like automatically.
Many controlled accounts can push a hashtag into the trends artificially.
Faking a citizens' movement is called **astroturfing**.
A **sock puppet** is a disguised account with a false identity.
The Internet Research Agency from St Petersburg became known as a “troll factory”.
Tools such as Botometer only give probabilities, not certainty.

abschnitte.text: A **social bot** is a program that operates an account on a platform such as X, Facebook or Instagram on its own. It can write posts, share, comment and like. Some bots are harmless and report the weather or the news, for example. It becomes a problem when a bot pretends to be a real person. Then readers can no longer tell who is really behind an opinion.

Many coordinated accounts can share a topic in huge numbers in a short time. This way a hashtag ends up in the **trends**, even though hardly any real people are interested in it. A topic then seems more important or more controversial than it is among the population. If a citizens' movement is only faked in this way, it is called **astroturfing**. The name comes from the artificial grass brand AstroTurf and is a play on real “grassroots movements”.

A **sock puppet** is a second account that a person uses to fake a false identity. This creates seemingly independent voices that support the person's own opinion. If many such accounts are controlled automatically, they are called bots. A **troll factory** runs a very large number of fake accounts at once. The **Internet Research Agency** from St Petersburg became well known; according to the report by special counsel Robert Mueller, it tried to influence the mood before the 2016 US election.

A typical sign is an account that publishes a very large number of posts around the clock. People sleep and post irregularly; bots need no break. Other signs are new accounts, names with lots of numbers and texts that are always the same. Indiana University has developed the tool **Botometer**, which analyses activity, network and language. But it only calculates a probability and can be wrong.

As early as 1950, the mathematician **Alan Turing** presented the imitation game, now called the Turing test. In it, a person has to find out in a text conversation whether they are talking to a human or a machine. Modern chatbots now write very naturally. That is why it is becoming harder and harder to tell bots from humans. This makes it all the more important to check sources and not to trust every account blindly.

gewusst: The word “bot” is short for “robot”.
The term astroturfing comes from a brand of artificial grass.
The Turing test was thought up as early as 1950, long before there was social media.

teile.einleitung: The consultation procedure is an important step before a new law goes to parliament. In it, cantons, parties, associations and other interested parties may give their opinion on a draft. This is meant to produce a law that is supported by as many people as possible.
wichtigste: In the consultation, cantons, parties and associations give their opinion on a draft law.
It takes place before the law goes to parliament.
A consultation usually lasts about three months.
Any person or organisation may send in an opinion.
After that, the administration evaluates the replies.
The procedure is a typical part of Swiss consensus democracy.

abschnitte.text: When the Confederation plans a new law or a change to the constitution, the administration first writes a **draft**. Before it goes to parliament, the Federal Council sends it out for **consultation**. The German word “Vernehmlassung” comes from “sich vernehmen lassen”, that is, to make your opinion heard. The cantons also have such procedures for their own laws.

Those invited are mainly the cantons, the political parties and the umbrella organisations of municipalities, cities and business. On top of that come organisations that are particularly affected by the topic, such as environmental groups or trade unions. But any individual person may also submit an **opinion**. The documents are publicly available on the internet.

A consultation usually lasts three months. After that, the administration sums up all the replies in a **report on the results**. The Federal Council decides whether to change the draft. Then it sends it to parliament with a dispatch.

The consultation helps to spot problems and mistakes early. The Confederation finds out what the cantons, which often have to put the laws into practice, think of it. You can also see whether a **referendum** is likely if important groups are against it. This produces laws that are more likely to be a **compromise**.

The consultation procedure is anchored in the **Federal Constitution**. It is set out in more detail in the Consultation Procedure Act, which has applied since 2005. Critics sometimes say the procedure makes laws slow. Supporters think it strengthens direct democracy.

begriffe.erklaerung: A procedure in which you can give your opinion on a draft law.
A written view on a proposal.
The first version of a law, which can still be changed.
The Federal Council's explanation of a law to parliament.

gewusst: For controversial proposals, hundreds or even thousands of opinions sometimes come in during a consultation.
The consultation is a Swiss peculiarity that exists in this form in few other countries.

teile.einleitung: The right to vote is the right to say yes or no in votes. Together with the right to elect, it is one of the most important political rights in Switzerland. People who have it are said to be entitled to vote.
wichtigste: With the right to vote, you say yes or no in votes.
With the right to elect, you choose people for a political office.
At federal level, Swiss citizens aged 18 and over are entitled to vote.
The federal voting age used to be 20; in 1991 it was lowered to 18.
All voters are listed in their municipality's electoral register.
Your vote is secret: nobody has to reveal how they voted.
The canton of Schaffhausen has compulsory voting.

abschnitte.text: The **right to vote** allows you to help decide on proposals in votes. The **right to elect** allows you to choose people, for example for the **National Council**. Both belong together and are known together as political rights. Anyone who may vote and elect at federal level can also be elected to the National Council themselves from the age of 18.

For a long time you could only vote at federal level at **20**. On **3 March 1991** voters accepted a **voting age of 18**. Since then all Swiss citizens aged 18 and over have been able to take part at federal level. On cantonal questions the cantons can decide for themselves; Glarus, for example, already lets 16-year-olds take part.

Each municipality keeps an **electoral register**. It lists all the people who may vote in the municipality. Only those who are registered receive the voting papers at home. **Swiss citizens living abroad** can also register in a Swiss municipality.

In ballot box votes, the **secrecy of the ballot** applies. Nobody may demand that you reveal your vote. In most cantons voting is voluntary. But the canton of **Schaffhausen** has **compulsory voting**: anyone who does not vote without a good reason pays a small amount.

At federal level, people with **Swiss citizenship** aged 18 and over are entitled to vote. At the 2023 elections there were about **5.6 million** of them, including Swiss citizens abroad. Children and foreign residents may not vote at federal level. But some cantons and municipalities give foreigners a right to vote on their own questions.

gewusst: Women only got the right to vote and elect at federal level in 1971.
In Switzerland you can vote on proposals several times every year, more often than in almost any other country.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who wants to support a popular initiative or a referendum signs on a signature form. The law sets out exactly what must be on this form.
wichtigste: At the top of the form are the title and the exact text of the initiative.
You write your surname, first name, date of birth and address and sign.
Each person signs themselves and by hand.
Only people from the same political municipality may sign on one form.
The municipality of residence checks whether someone is entitled to vote.
You may only sign once for the same initiative.

abschnitte.titel: What is at the top of the form
abschnitte.text: Each form shows the **title** and the **exact text** of the initiative. That way you know what you are signing for. There is also the date on which the text was published in the Federal Gazette and the names of the initiators. There is also a note that **forging** signatures is a criminal offence. The canton and the political municipality of the people signing are given too.

On one line you write your **surname, first name, date of birth** and **address**. Then comes your own **signature**. Each person must sign themselves and **by hand**. Nobody may sign for another person. You may only sign **once** for the same initiative; double signatures are invalid.

Only people from the **same political municipality** may sign on one form. The reason: each municipality only checks its own residents. If someone lives in a different municipality, they need a form of their own. That is why people collecting signatures often carry forms for different municipalities. If you print out a form, you fill in your own municipality yourself.

The completed forms go to the **municipality of residence**. It looks in the electoral register to see whether the people live there and may vote. It confirms this on the form; this is called the **certificate of voting rights**. Only after that are the forms submitted to the **Federal Chancellery**. At the end it counts whether enough valid signatures have been collected.

gewusst: A signature can be invalid if the name cannot be read or the person lives in a different municipality from the one stated on the form.
Forms from the internet are valid too, as long as you print them out and sign them by hand.

teile.einleitung: Unterbäch is a small mountain village in the canton of Valais that has gone down in Swiss history. Here, on 3 March 1957, women were allowed to take part in a federal vote for the first time in Switzerland. And this even though votes for women were still forbidden nationally at the time.
wichtigste: Unterbäch is a municipality in Upper Valais.
In 1957 the authorities there were the first in Switzerland to let women vote.
At that time votes for women were not yet allowed nationally.
The women's votes went into a separate ballot box and did not count.
Even so, the action became an important signal for equal rights.
Only in 1971 did Swiss women get the right to vote at federal level.
That is why Unterbäch is sometimes called the “Rütli of Swiss women”.

abschnitte.text: **Unterbäch** lies on a sunny terrace above the Rhône valley in the district of Western Raron. The village is at about 1200 metres above sea level. From here you can see the Valais Alps, such as the Bietschhorn. Unterbäch has only a few hundred inhabitants, who speak Valais German.

On 3 March 1957 Switzerland voted on an article about **civil protection**. Because this would also have obliged women to serve, many people felt that women should have a say. The municipal council of Unterbäch therefore decided to let the women vote. The idea came from the Valais politician Peter von Roten, the husband of the women's rights campaigner Iris von Roten.

abschnitte.titel: The first women at the ballot box
abschnitte.text: The first woman to cast her ballot was **Katharina Zenhäusern**, the wife of the municipal president. In all, 33 of 84 women entitled to vote took part. Their votes were collected in a separate ballot box. The Confederation declared them invalid, but the signal had been sent.

The action caused a great stir all over Switzerland and even abroad. Many newspapers reported on it; some praised the courage, others criticised the breaking of the law. Journalists from other countries also came to the small village. This gave new momentum to the debate about **votes for women**.

abschnitte.titel: The long road to the vote
abschnitte.text: In the first federal vote on votes for women in 1959, the men still clearly said no. Only on 7 February 1971 were votes for women accepted at federal level. The last canton, Appenzell Innerrhoden, had to introduce them in 1990 on the orders of the **Federal Supreme Court**. To this day Unterbäch is regarded as a symbol of this struggle.

Today Unterbäch is a quiet village for holidays and walking. A cable car links it to Raron in the valley. In winter there are ski slopes in the **Brandalp** area. Memorial plaques and anniversary celebrations in the village recall the vote of 1957.

begriffe.erklaerung: The right of women to vote and to elect.
An organisation that protects the population in disasters.
The government of a municipality.
A container into which you put the ballot papers.

gewusst: Switzerland only introduced votes for women at federal level in 1971, decades after most countries in Europe.
The women of Unterbäch voted in 1957, a full 14 years before votes for women nationally.

teile.einleitung: The principle of proportionality requires the state not to intervene more strongly than necessary. A measure must fit its aim and must not place an excessive burden on those affected.
wichtigste: All state action must be proportionate, as Art. 5 para. 2 of the Federal Constitution requires.
The principle has three parts: suitability, necessity and reasonableness.
A measure is suitable if it can achieve the aim.
It is necessary if there is no milder means that is just as effective.
For reasonableness, public and private interests are weighed against each other.
A well-known image for a breach: shooting at sparrows with cannons.

abschnitte.text: **Art. 5 para. 2** of the Federal Constitution requires state action to be in the **public interest** and **proportionate**. This applies to the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities. The principle is especially important when the state restricts **fundamental rights**. According to **Art. 36**, every such restriction must be proportionate. Courts often check this when someone challenges a measure.

First you ask whether the measure is **suitable**. It must be able to achieve the intended aim at all. A measure that is **unfit** for the aim may not be ordered. An example: a ban that changes nothing about the problem is never proportionate. So suitability is the first hurdle.

Then **necessity** is checked. If there is a **milder means** that achieves the aim just as well, the state must choose it. An example: because of a single noise complaint, a municipality bans all concerts for a year. The ban would certainly prevent noise. But time limits or volume restrictions would be enough, so the total ban is not necessary.

Finally comes **proportionality in the narrower sense**, also called **reasonableness**. Here things are weighed up: how great is the benefit for the public, and how serious is the intrusion for the person affected? If the two are not in a sensible relationship, the measure is disproportionate. The German saying **“shooting at sparrows with cannons”** (in English, “using a sledgehammer to crack a nut”) describes exactly such a case. The means is far too strong for the small problem.

gewusst: A measure must meet all three parts: if it fails even one of them, it is disproportionate.
The principle of proportionality applies not only to laws but also to individual decisions by authorities, such as a fine or a permit.

teile.einleitung: The majority of the cantons (in German “Ständemehr”) is the majority of the cantons in a popular vote. In important votes, for example on changes to the Federal Constitution, it is not enough for the majority of the people to say yes. The majority of the cantons must also agree.
wichtigste: The majority of the cantons means that most cantons must agree.
The vote of a canton is called a cantonal vote.
There are 23 cantonal votes in total.
Six cantons have only half a cantonal vote.
The result in the canton decides how its cantonal vote counts.
Changes to the constitution need a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons.
The majority of the cantons protects the small cantons.

abschnitte.titel: What is the majority of the cantons?
abschnitte.text: In the past the cantons were called **Stände** (estates). That is why the majority of the cantons is called the Ständemehr in German. In a vote, the votes are counted in each canton to see whether more yes or more no votes were cast there. The result decides how that canton's **cantonal vote** counts.

20 cantons have one whole cantonal vote each. Six cantons have only **half a cantonal vote**: Obwalden, Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden. Together that makes 23 cantonal votes. So a yes needs at least 12 cantonal votes; at 11.5 to 11.5 a proposal is rejected.

The majority of the cantons is needed for all changes to the **Federal Constitution**. That is why every accepted popular initiative also needs the majority of the cantons. On top of that come joining certain international organisations and certain urgent laws. For ordinary laws, however, the **majority of the people** is enough.

The majority of the cantons was introduced in 1848 with the Federal Constitution. It is meant to prevent the large cantons from simply outvoting the small ones. This way a vote in Uri or Appenzell Innerrhoden carries more weight in the majority of the cantons than a vote in Zurich. This is an expression of **federalism**.

abschnitte.titel: When the people and the cantons disagree
abschnitte.text: Sometimes the people say yes, but the majority of the cantons says no. This happened, for example, in 2020 with the responsible business initiative. About 50.7 per cent of voters said yes, but the majority of the cantons rejected it. So the initiative failed.

begriffe.erklaerung: An old word for canton.
The vote of a canton in the majority of the cantons.
The majority of all voters in the whole of Switzerland.
The former name for the cantons with half a cantonal vote.

gewusst: A canton with a few thousand voters has as much weight in the majority of the cantons as the canton of Zurich with over a million inhabitants.
In theory a proposal could fail because of the majority of the cantons, even though a clear majority of the people say yes.
Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft have only half cantonal votes because they used to be one canton.

teile.einleitung: A ballot paper is a piece of paper on which you give your opinion in a vote. For example, you tick yes or no or write it in a box. Then you put it in a ballot box or send it back by post.
wichtigste: On the ballot paper you give yes or no in a vote.
There is a separate question on the ballot paper for each proposal.
For elections people usually speak of an election ballot.
The ballot paper goes into a voting envelope so that nobody sees how you voted.
You can put the paper in the ballot box or vote by post.
If you write something wrong on the paper, you make it invalid.
The secrecy of the ballot protects your own decision.

abschnitte.text: The **ballot paper** is the most important piece of paper in a vote. It shows the question being voted on, for example “Do you accept the new law?”. Next to it there is a box for the answer. Depending on the paper, you tick yes or no or write the word in.

Before a vote, all voters receive the papers at home. They include the ballot papers, the voting card and a voting booklet with explanations. You fill in the paper and put it in the **voting envelope**. Then you put it in the **ballot box** at the polling station or send it back by post.

Nobody may find out how someone voted. This is called the **secrecy of the ballot**. That is why the ballot paper goes into a separate envelope, apart from the signed voting card. That way you can decide freely, without pressure from others.

If you do not write an answer, you hand in a **blank** ballot paper. It does not count as yes or no in the count. If you put insults or drawings on the paper, you make it invalid. A paper on which you cannot tell what is meant does not count either.

After voting Sunday, helpers in the **electoral office** count all the papers. Today ballot papers are often counted by machines too. The municipalities' results are reported to the canton and the Confederation. By the evening of voting Sunday the result is usually already known.

In votes on issues, people use ballot papers with yes and no. In elections of people there are **election ballots** on which you write names. In National Council elections each party has its own list. You can cross out names or even write them twice; this is called cumulation.

begriffe.erklaerung: A paper on which you give your answer in a vote.
A sealed container for the ballot papers.
Nobody may know how someone voted.
A group that counts the votes.

gewusst: In federal votes in Switzerland, people traditionally write “Ja” (yes) or “Nein” (no) by hand in the box.
At a Landsgemeinde there is no ballot paper at all; people vote by raising their hands.
If there is an initiative and a counter-proposal, the ballot paper also has a tie-break question.

tppikys.t: Number of signatures for a popular initiative

teile.einleitung: A federal popular initiative needs 100,000 valid signatures. They must be collected within 18 months, otherwise the initiative fails.
wichtigste: A popular initiative needs at least 100,000 valid signatures.
The time limit for collecting is 18 months, that is, a year and a half.
A hundred thousand is written as a 1 with five zeros: 100,000.
More signatures than needed are allowed.
Because some signatures are invalid, it is better to collect a few more.
With enough valid signatures, the initiative has “succeeded”.

abschnitte.text: A hundred thousand is written as the number **100,000**, that is, a 1 with five zeros. A federal popular initiative needs this many **valid signatures**. That is the **minimum**; more is allowed. So an initiative may also be submitted with 150,000 signatures. With 80,000, however, it is not enough; then 20,000 are still missing.

From the publication in the Federal Gazette, a committee has **18 months**. A year has 12 months, and 12 plus 6 makes 18, so that is **a year and a half**. Anyone who collects 10,000 valid signatures every month has enough after 10 months. Many committees collect a particularly large number at the beginning. That way there is time left at the end for checking.

Not every signature counts. It is **invalid**, for example, if someone is not **entitled to vote** or has signed twice. That is why committees usually collect a lot more than 100,000. If valid signatures are missing at the end of the time limit, the initiative **fails**. Then there is no vote.

The **Federal Chancellery** counts the signatures and checks them. If there are enough valid ones, the initiative has **“succeeded”**. After that the Federal Council and parliament debate it. They can give a recommendation or make a counter-proposal. In the end **the people and the cantons** decide at the ballot box.

gewusst: Until 1977, 50,000 signatures were enough for a popular initiative; then the number was doubled to 100,000.
The 18-month time limit for collecting has applied since 1978; before that there was no fixed time limit.

teile.einleitung: In a tacit election there is no round of voting. This is possible when no more people stand than there are seats available. All the candidates are then considered elected.
wichtigste: There is a **tacit election** when no more people stand than there are seats available.
Then all the candidates are considered elected without a vote.
A tacit election is also allowed in **National Council elections**.
Tacit elections are particularly common in **municipalities**.
In 2023 **Erich Ettlin** was elected tacitly to the Council of States in Obwalden.
Critics complain that the people have no choice.

abschnitte.text: Normally voters choose from several candidates. But if by the closing date no more people have come forward than there are seats available, no vote is needed. All the candidates are then considered **elected**. This is called a **tacit election**. An example: if a municipal council has 5 seats and 7 people come forward, the people must vote, because 7 is more than 5.

Article 45 of the **Federal Act on Political Rights** also allows tacit elections in National Council elections. If there are no more candidates than seats, the **cantonal government** declares them all elected. In practice, however, this rarely happens for the National Council. For **Council of States elections**, the cantons decide the procedure themselves. In 2023 only one person stood for the one seat in the Council of States in **Obwalden**.

The Centre politician **Erich Ettlin** was the only candidate for the Council of States in Obwalden in 2023. That is why he was elected tacitly. In 2019 too, nobody had stood against him. And yet the hurdle for standing in Obwalden is low: only **five signatures** from voters are needed. So a low hurdle does not guarantee a choice.

Tacit elections are especially common in **municipalities**. There it is sometimes difficult to find enough people for offices such as the **municipal council** or the **school authority**. Many of these offices are carried out alongside a job. If just as many people come forward as there are seats, no election takes place. This saves the municipality effort and costs.

Critics say that in a tacit election the voters have **no choice**. They cannot vote anyone out or prefer another person. Supporters stress that it saves money and time on an unnecessary vote. Anyone who wants to prevent a tacit election can **stand** themselves or put forward another person. Then a real vote is needed.

gewusst: Erich Ettlin got into the Council of States twice in a row without anyone standing against him.
A single extra candidate is enough to turn a tacit election into a real election.

teile.einleitung: Insurance protects against the consequences of bad luck, for example in case of illness, an accident or damage. Many people pay in regularly, and anyone who suffers a loss gets money from the shared pot.
wichtigste: For insurance you regularly pay a premium.
Basic health insurance has been compulsory for everyone in Switzerland since 1996.
Liability insurance pays for damage you cause to others by accident.
Every car needs motor vehicle liability insurance.
Household contents insurance protects the things in your home.
Employees are insured against accidents through accident insurance.

abschnitte.text: With insurance, **many people** regularly pay in an amount. This amount is called a **premium**, and you pay it, for example, every month or every year. The money goes into a shared pot. If someone suffers a loss, they get money from it. This way many people help together when individuals have bad luck.

**Basic health insurance** is **compulsory** in Switzerland, for children and babies too. This has been the case since **1996**, when the **Health Insurance Act** came into force. The health insurer pays, for example, for visits to the doctor, medicines and stays in hospital. At the doctor's surgery you show your **insurance card**. It shows which health insurer you are insured with.

If you break your neighbour's window by accident, **liability insurance** pays. It covers damage that you cause to **others**. Many families have private liability insurance, but it is not compulsory. It is different for **cars**: **motor vehicle liability insurance** is required for every car. It pays for damage that you cause to others with the car.

**Household contents insurance** pays for things in your home that are stolen or damaged. These include furniture, clothes and appliances, for example after a burglary or water damage. Anyone who is **employed** is insured against **accidents** by law. Accident insurance then pays for things like the doctor and hospital. The **AVS** is also a form of insurance; it helps mainly in old age.

gewusst: In most cantons buildings must be insured against fire and natural hazards, often with a cantonal building insurer.
With health insurance you pay part of the costs yourself; this is called the excess (in Switzerland “Franchise”).

teile.einleitung: The public prosecutor's office is the authority that prosecutes crimes. It leads the investigation, collects evidence and decides whether a case goes to court. In Switzerland every canton has its own public prosecutor's office, and the Confederation has the Office of the Attorney General.
wichtigste: Since 2011 a single **Criminal Procedure Code** has applied throughout Switzerland.
The public prosecutor's office leads the **criminal investigation** for adults.
The **police** often investigate on behalf of the public prosecutor's office.
With a **penalty order** the public prosecutor's office can settle minor cases itself.
You can lodge an **objection** to a penalty order within ten days.
The federal public prosecutor's office is called the **Office of the Attorney General**.

abschnitte.text: In the past, every canton had its own rules for criminal proceedings. On 1 January **2011** the **Swiss Criminal Procedure Code** came into force. Since then criminal proceedings have followed the same rules throughout Switzerland. But the courts and authorities mostly remain a matter for the cantons. That is why every canton has its own public prosecutor's office.

If a crime is suspected, the **public prosecutor's office** leads the investigation. The **police** look for clues, question people and collect evidence. In doing so they follow the instructions of the public prosecutor's office. The **presumption of innocence** is important: until there is a verdict, an accused person is considered innocent. If the suspicion is not confirmed, the public prosecutor's office closes the case with a **ruling to abandon proceedings**.

If a case is clear and fairly minor, the public prosecutor's office can set a penalty itself. This is called a **penalty order**. It is possible, for example, for a prison sentence of at most six months. Most criminal proceedings in Switzerland end with a penalty order, without a court hearing. Anyone who disagrees can lodge an **objection** within ten days; then there is usually a court case.

In more serious cases a **court** has to decide. Then the public prosecutor's office brings an **indictment**. In court it represents the public's interest in prosecuting the crime. The accused person can be defended by a lawyer. In the end the court gives the verdict, not the public prosecutor's office.

abschnitte.titel: The Office of the Attorney General
abschnitte.text: The Confederation is responsible for certain crimes. These are prosecuted by the **Office of the Attorney General**, based in Bern. It brings its indictments before the **Federal Criminal Court** in Bellinzona. For young people there are special rules and separate authorities, the **juvenile prosecutor's offices**. There the main focus is on education and not on punishment.

gewusst: Most criminal proceedings in Switzerland never go to court at all, but end with a penalty order.
The Federal Criminal Court is not in Bern, but in Bellinzona in Ticino.

teile.einleitung: For a popular initiative or a referendum to succeed, many signatures are needed. Committees and volunteers collect them in the street, at stands and over the internet.
wichtigste: Many collectors stand in streets and squares with forms and biros.
Signing is always voluntary.
Only voters aged 18 and over may sign a federal initiative.
You can print out many forms on the internet and send them back by post.
Forging signatures is forbidden and a criminal offence.
Completed forms go back to the committee.

abschnitte.text: Most signatures are collected directly from people. Collectors stand in **squares**, at stations or outside shops. They often have a small **stand** with posters. They carry **signature forms** and biros. They speak to people and briefly explain what their idea is about.

If someone understands an idea and likes it, they are more likely to sign. That is why the collectors **explain** their cause. But signing is always **voluntary**. Anyone who does not agree can simply say no. A signature only means that you want a vote, not how you will vote later.

Many committees put their forms on the **internet**. You can **print out** a form at home, fill it in by hand and sign it. Then you send it back to the committee **by post**. Only forms that are sent back can be counted. Some committees also send out forms with newspapers or letters.

Only **voters** may sign, that is, Swiss citizens aged **18** and over. A child may therefore not sign yet, but can help hand out leaflets. Anyone who **forges** signatures commits a criminal offence. Every form points this out too. In many municipalities you need a permit for stands on public land.

gewusst: Because some signatures are invalid, committees usually collect a lot more than they need.
Many municipalities require a permit for collecting at a stand on public land.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Broadcasting Corporation, SRG for short, makes radio, television and online content in all four national languages. It has a mission known as “public service”. It is funded mainly by the radio and television fee.
wichtigste: The SRG broadcasts in German, French, Italian and Romansh.
Its companies are called SRF, RTS, RSI and RTR.
Swissinfo informs the world about Switzerland in ten languages.
Play Suisse shows Swiss films and series with subtitles.
Since 2021 a private household has paid a fee of 335 francs a year.
Since November 2024 Susanne Wille has been Director General.

abschnitte.text: The SRG is made up of several companies. **SRF** broadcasts in German, **RTS** in French and **RSI** in Italian. **RTR** stands for Radiotelevisiun Svizra Rumantscha and broadcasts in Romansh. There is also **Swissinfo**, which informs Swiss people living abroad and an international audience in ten languages.

Article 93 of the **Federal Constitution** describes what radio and television should achieve. They should contribute to **education**, cultural development, the **free forming of opinions** and entertainment. In doing so, they must take into account the special features of the country and the needs of the cantons. This mission is called **public service**.

**Play Suisse** is a streaming platform of the SRG. It has Swiss films, series and documentaries from all language regions. They are subtitled in several national languages. So you can, for example, follow a series from Ticino with German subtitles. This is meant to encourage exchange between the language regions.

Almost all households pay the **radio and television fee**. Since 2021 it has been 335 francs a year for a private household. The Federal Council has decided to lower it step by step to 312 francs from 2027 and 300 francs from 2029. The SRG receives most of it, because it has to offer a comparable service in all four national languages. The smaller language regions receive more money than they bring in themselves. Local private broadcasters also receive a share.

The SRG is run by a **Director General**. Since November 2024 this has been **Susanne Wille**. She followed Gilles Marchand. Before that, from 2020, she was head of culture at SRF and a member of its executive board.

gewusst: The small Romansh-speaking region has its own radio and television with RTR.
Because all language regions are meant to be served equally well, money flows from German-speaking Switzerland to the smaller regions.

tswkxw2.t: Distribution of seats in the National Council

teile.einleitung: The National Council has 200 seats. They are shared out among the cantons according to the number of people living in each canton. Large cantons therefore have many seats, small ones only a few.
wichtigste: Since 1962 the National Council has been fixed at 200 seats.
The seats are shared out using the Hare/Niemeyer method.
The basis is the permanent resident population; foreign residents also count.
Every canton has at least one seat.
At the 2023 election six cantons had only one seat.
For the 2023 election one seat went from Basel-Stadt to Zurich.

abschnitte.text: In the past, the National Council grew with the population, because there was one seat for a fixed number of inhabitants. Since a **constitutional amendment in 1962**, exactly **200 seats** are always shared out. The seats are divided among the cantons according to the **permanent resident population**. This also includes foreign residents, even though they are not allowed to vote at federal level. Every canton receives at least one seat.

Sharing out the seats needs a rule of calculation. Switzerland uses the **Hare/Niemeyer** method. First, it is worked out exactly how many seats a canton would be entitled to. Usually this does not give a whole number. Each canton first gets its whole seats. The remaining seats go to the cantons with the largest **remainders** after the decimal point.

At the 2023 election **Zurich** had the most seats, namely 36. It was followed by **Bern** with 24, **Vaud** with 19 and **Aargau** with 16. **St Gallen** and **Geneva** had 12 seats each. Six cantons had only one seat: Uri, Obwalden, Nidwalden, Glarus, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden. There, one seat cannot be divided by percentages. That is why the vote uses the **majority system**: the person with the most votes wins.

If the population of a canton grows faster than elsewhere, it can gain seats. Other cantons then lose seats. For the 2023 election, one seat went from **Basel-Stadt** to **Zurich**. Since then Basel-Stadt has had four seats instead of five. **Bern** still had 33 seats in 1963, but only 24 in 2023. That is 9 seats fewer, because other cantons have grown faster.

gewusst: The canton of Bern has lost nine National Council seats since 1963, even though its population has grown.
People without a Swiss passport also count when the seats are shared out among the cantons.

teile.einleitung: With the Declaration of Independence in 1776, thirteen British colonies in North America broke away from Great Britain. This gave rise to the United States of America.
wichtigste: The Declaration was adopted in Philadelphia on 4 July 1776.
Its main author was Thomas Jefferson.
It was passed by the Second Continental Congress.
13 colonies declared themselves independent of Great Britain and King George III.
It names life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness as unalienable rights.
56 men signed the Declaration.

abschnitte.text: The 13 colonies on the east coast of North America belonged to **Great Britain**. Many settlers were angry about taxes and laws decided in London. They themselves had no representatives in parliament there. The dispute with King **George III** grew more and more bitter. In 1775 the War of Independence began.

Representatives of all the colonies sat in the **Second Continental Congress**. It met in **Philadelphia**, in the building now called Independence Hall. A committee was given the task of writing a declaration. **Thomas Jefferson** wrote the draft, and Benjamin Franklin and John Adams helped to revise it. On 4 July 1776 Congress adopted the text.

The Declaration says that **all men are created equal**. They have rights that cannot be taken away from them: **life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness**. A government exists to protect these rights. After that, the text lists many accusations against the King. At the end the colonies declare themselves free and independent states.

**56 men** signed the Declaration, most of them on 2 August 1776. Very large in the middle is the name of **John Hancock**, the President of Congress. That is why in the USA people say “John Hancock” when they mean a signature. Jefferson later became the third President of the USA. Today 4 July is the national holiday, **Independence Day**.

gewusst: The 13 stripes on the flag of the USA are still a reminder of the 13 founding colonies.
Thomas Jefferson and John Adams both died on 4 July 1826, exactly 50 years after the Declaration.

teile.einleitung: Tolerance means letting other people be as they are. You do not have to like everything, but you accept other opinions and ways of life. Tolerance is important for living together peacefully.
wichtigste: Tolerance means accepting other opinions and ways of life.
The opposite is called intolerance.
The International Day for Tolerance is on 16 November.
In Switzerland everyone may choose their religion freely.
You do not have to agree with everyone, but you stay friendly.

abschnitte.text: **Tolerance** means accepting other **opinions**, habits or ways of life. The word comes from the Latin **“tolerare”**, which means “to bear” or “to endure”. You do not have to like everything. But you allow it and treat others with **respect**.

People have different **preferences**, such as a different favourite colour. Some do not eat certain things, for example no **pork** because of their religion. Someone who simply accepts this is tolerant. If a child speaks a different **mother tongue**, **patient listening** helps. Anyone learning a new language still makes mistakes.

The opposite of tolerance is **intolerance**. The prefix “in” here means “not”. Intolerant people do not accept others. For example, they laugh at them or leave them out. Different opinions are normal. What matters is that people still treat each other in a **friendly** way and without insults.

In Switzerland people with different **languages**, religions and traditions live together. **Freedom of religion** is set out in the **Federal Constitution**. Everyone may believe what they wish, or belong to no religion at all. The constitution also forbids putting people at a disadvantage because of their origin or language.

In **1995** **UNESCO** declared **16 November** the **International Day for Tolerance**. On this day people around the world think about living together peacefully. Schools and organisations use it to talk about respect and diversity.

gewusst: Tolerance has limits: anyone who harms others or uses violence does not have to be tolerated.
In engineering, “tolerance” means the permitted deviation from a measurement.

teile.einleitung: Table manners are rules about how to behave when eating. They make sure that everyone at the table feels comfortable. Many rules also have to do with cleanliness and consideration.
wichtigste: You wash your hands before eating.
In German-speaking Switzerland people wish each other “En Guete”.
You say “please” and “thank you”.
You do not talk with your mouth full.
The fork goes to the left of the plate, the knife to the right.
You should cough or sneeze into the crook of your arm.
After the meal you take your plate to the kitchen.

abschnitte.text: Before eating, you **wash** your hands with soap. That way fewer **germs** get into the food. In **German-speaking Switzerland** people then wish each other **“En Guete”**, which means “Enjoy your meal”. In French-speaking Switzerland people say “Bon appétit”, in Ticino “Buon appetito”. Often you wait until everyone is sitting at the table.

When **laying the table**, you put the **fork on the left** and the **knife on the right** of the plate. The blade of the knife points towards the plate. The spoon usually lies to the right of the knife or above the plate. The glass stands at the top right. Helping to lay the table is a good little **household job** (in Swiss German an “Ämtli”).

If you would like something passed to you, you say **“please”**. When you get it, you say **“thank you”**. You do not talk with your **mouth full**, because it is hard to understand and looks unappetising. You can also **choke**. If you have to cough or sneeze, you turn away and do it into the **crook of your arm**.

In many families you ask whether you may **get down from the table**, or you wait until everyone has finished. Then you take your own **plate to the kitchen**. If you clear away yourself, you help the family. That way the work is shared fairly.

gewusst: In some Asian countries people eat with chopsticks, and quite different table rules apply there.
When you have finished eating with a knife and fork, you often lay both side by side at an angle on the plate.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who signs a popular initiative or a referendum must be entitled to vote. The municipality where they live confirms this with the certificate of voting rights. Only then does a signature count.
wichtigste: The municipality of residence certifies that the signatories are entitled to vote.
For this it checks each signature against the electoral register.
Only people from the same municipality may sign on one signature list.
Surname, first name, date of birth and address help the municipality to find the person.
Each person may sign the same initiative only once.
Signing with someone else's name is a criminal offence.

abschnitte.text: A **popular initiative** needs signatures from voters. Whether a person really is entitled to vote is known by their **municipality of residence**. It keeps the **electoral register** and checks each signature. If everything is in order, it confirms the right to vote. This is called the **certificate of voting rights**.

Each list states the **political municipality**. Only voters from this municipality may sign it, because each municipality only checks its own register. Each person writes down their **surname, first name, date of birth and address**. Then comes their **handwritten signature**. Anyone who cannot write may have their name entered by another voter, who then signs themselves.

Initiative committees often have the signatures certified **while they are still collecting**. There is a reason for this: if a person has **moved away** or **died** in the meantime, the municipality can no longer confirm their right to vote. Then the signature does not count. Those who have signatures certified early lose fewer of them.

Each voter may sign the same request **only once**. Double signatures would distort the result. Anyone who **forges** someone else's signature or signs with a false name commits a **criminal offence**. **Swiss citizens living abroad** are certified by the municipality in whose electoral register they are listed.

gewusst: A federal popular initiative needs 100,000 valid signatures.
After the municipalities have certified them, the Federal Chancellery counts the signatures again.

teile.einleitung: A tie means that in a vote both sides have the same number of votes. Then nobody has won yet. A rule is needed to still reach a decision.
wichtigste: In a **tie** both sides have the same number of votes.
It is also called a **draw** or a **deadlock**.
In a tie, nobody has won yet.
With two proposals, a tie is only possible with an **even number** of votes.
You can **vote again** or provide for a casting vote.
A single vote can cause a tie or break it.

abschnitte.text: If 10 children vote yes and 10 children vote no, both sides have the same number of votes. This is called a **tie** or a **draw**. In votes people also speak of a **deadlock**; the German word “Patt” comes from chess, where it means stalemate. Neither side has more votes, so nobody has won yet. A tie shows that opinions in the group are split exactly in half.

If there are two proposals and everyone votes, a tie is only possible with an **even number**. In a class of 18 children, for example, there is a tie at **9 to 9**. With 21 children this is not possible if everyone votes. Even a single vote can change a lot. If it is 7 to 6 and a missing child later votes no, it is **7 to 7**.

In a tie, the group can talk about the proposals again. After that it can **vote again**, and sometimes some people change their minds. Another solution is the **casting vote**: a person chosen beforehand tips the balance. Sometimes **drawing lots** decides. What matters is that everyone knows the rule beforehand.

Ties can happen in parliaments too. In the National Council, the president of the chamber then gives the casting vote. That way parliament can still reach a decision. Municipalities and cantons also have fixed rules for this. They are usually set out in law or in the rules of procedure.

gewusst: The German word “Patt” comes from chess, where a game ends without a winner.
With an odd number of votes and two proposals, there can be no tie if everyone votes.

teile.einleitung: The form of state describes how a state is built up and who is at the top. For example, you ask: is there a king, is the head of state elected, or does one person rule without free elections? Switzerland is a republic and a federal state with direct democracy.
wichtigste: The form of state describes how a state is built up.
In a monarchy a king or queen is head of state.
In a republic the head of state is not a monarch.
A federal state is made up of member states with a shared federal government.
In a dictatorship one person or group rules without free elections.
Liechtenstein is a constitutional monarchy.
Vatican City is an absolute elective monarchy.

abschnitte.text: In a **monarchy** a king, a queen or a prince is head of state. The office is usually inherited within one family. In a constitutional monarchy the monarch's power is limited by a constitution. Examples are the United Kingdom, Sweden, Spain and Liechtenstein.

In a **republic** there is no monarch. The head of state, for example a president, is elected for a certain period. Most countries in the world today are republics, such as France, Germany, Italy and the USA. Switzerland is also a republic.

A **federal state** is made up of member states that carry out many tasks themselves. In Switzerland these are the 26 cantons, in Germany and Austria the federal states (Länder), in the USA the states. In contrast, a unitary state such as France is governed more strongly from the capital. Switzerland has been a federal state since 1848.

In a **dictatorship** one person or a small group rules without free elections and almost without limits. Criticising the government is often forbidden, and the press is not free. Courts are not independent. The opposite of this is democracy, in which the people hold power.

Our neighbour **Liechtenstein** is a constitutional monarchy with a prince at the top and an elected parliament, the Landtag. But the prince there has more rights than monarchs in most other European countries. Vatican City in Rome is an absolute **elective monarchy**. Its head is the Pope, who is elected by the cardinals and holds all power.

Switzerland is a republic, a federal state and a **direct democracy**. There is no single person as head of state; the Federal Council as a body takes on this role. The people elect parliament and vote regularly on specific issues. This mixture is almost unique in the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: The person or group who represents the state to the outside world.
A form of state with a king, a queen or a prince.
A form of state without a monarch; the head is elected.
Dividing power between the federal level and the member states.

gewusst: With less than half a square kilometre, Vatican City is the smallest state in the world.
Liechtenstein is one of the few countries where the prince can block laws with his veto.
The word republic comes from the Latin “res publica” and means “public matter”.

teile.einleitung: A club (or association) is a group of people who join together for a shared aim. In Switzerland there are a great many clubs, from the gymnastics club to the brass band.
wichtigste: In a choir people sing together; in a brass band they play wind music.
In a gymnastics club people do sport together.
Every club has statutes, that is, written rules.
The president leads the club, and the treasurer manages the money.
All members meet at the general meeting.
Members usually pay a membership fee every year.

abschnitte.text: In many Swiss villages there are all sorts of clubs. In a **choir** people sing songs together, for example in the church choir. The **brass band** plays wind music at village festivals. In the **gymnastics club** people do sport together, and there is often a children's group. The **Samaritan association** learns first aid and helps at festivals and sporting events.

Every club writes down its rules in its **statutes**. They say what the club is for and how decisions are made. The **Civil Code** sets out how a club is founded. It needs an aim that is not about making a profit, and written statutes. Then the club is a **legal person** in its own right.

The club is run by the **committee**. The **president** leads the club and the meetings. The **treasurer** manages the money and writes down all income and spending. There is often also a secretary who writes the minutes. Most offices are carried out voluntarily and without pay.

All members meet at the **general meeting**. They elect the committee and decide on important questions. Each member has one vote. Members usually pay a **membership fee** every year. With it the club buys equipment, for example, or pays for courses.

gewusst: Many people learn for the first time in a club how to vote, elect and chair a meeting.
With freedom of association, the Federal Constitution protects the right to found clubs and to join them.

teile.einleitung: Travail.Suisse is an umbrella organisation of employees' organisations in Switzerland. It represents the concerns of employees to employers and politicians. After the Swiss Trade Union Federation, it is the second-largest umbrella organisation of employees.
wichtigste: Travail.Suisse was founded in Bern on 14 December 2002.
It grew out of the CNG and the VSA.
It is the second-largest umbrella organisation of employees.
Its member associations together represent about 150,000 members.
Syna is its largest member union.
OCST, Transfair and Hotel & Gastro Union also belong to it.

abschnitte.text: An **umbrella organisation** is a union of several associations. In the case of **Travail.Suisse**, these are trade unions and employees' associations. They campaign for good **wages**, fair **working conditions** and social security. The umbrella organisation represents their shared concerns in politics, for example in votes.

Travail.Suisse was founded in **Bern** on **14 December 2002**. The organisation grew out of the **Christian National Trade Union Federation (CNG)** and the **Federation of Swiss Employees' Associations (VSA)**. Their associations joined together under a new roof. This makes Travail.Suisse much younger than the **Swiss Trade Union Federation (SGB)**.

The largest member union is **Syna**. From Ticino, the **OCST** belongs to it. **Transfair** represents employees in the **public service**, for example at Swiss Post, the SBB and Swisscom. The **Hotel & Gastro Union** represents employees in hotels and catering. Together the associations represent about **150,000** members.

The largest umbrella organisation of employees is the **SGB**, with over 300,000 members. It includes, for example, **Unia**, the **VPOD**, the **SEV** and **Syndicom**. Travail.Suisse is the **second-largest** umbrella organisation. On the other side are the **employers'** associations, such as Gastrosuisse or Hotelleriesuisse in the hospitality industry.

gewusst: The name Travail.Suisse combines the French word for work with the name of Switzerland.
Several member associations of Travail.Suisse have Christian social roots.

teile.einleitung: The Council of States represents the cantons in the federal parliament. Its 46 members are elected in the cantons, usually on the same day as the National Council. Each canton decides for itself exactly how the election works.
wichtigste: The Council of States has 46 seats.
The Federal Constitution leaves the Council of States election to the cantons.
In most cantons you need an absolute majority in the first round.
Appenzell Innerrhoden elects its member of the Council of States in April at the Landsgemeinde.
In 2023 a second round was needed for 13 seats.
After the 2023 elections, the Centre was the strongest party in the Council of States with 15 seats.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Constitution** leaves the Council of States election to the **cantons**. That is why **cantonal law** applies to it, in Zurich, for example, the cantonal law on political rights. Most cantons have **two seats**, some cantons only one. You may write down at most as many names as there are seats to fill.

In most cantons the **majority vote** applies. In the **first round** you have to reach the **absolute majority**, that is, more than half of the votes that count. Anyone who misses it has to go into a **second round**. There, the **relative majority** is usually enough: whoever has the most votes is elected.

**Appenzell Innerrhoden** elects its member of the Council of States at the **Landsgemeinde**. This takes place in **April**, months before the other cantons. In April 2023 the Landsgemeinde confirmed **Daniel Fässler** of the Centre. That is why on election Sunday in October 2023 only **45** of the 46 seats were filled.

On **22 October 2023** the absolute majority was not reached for **13 seats**. The second rounds took place in November. After that, the **Centre** had 15 seats, the **FDP** 11, the **SP** 9 and the **SVP** 6. The **Mouvement Citoyens Genevois** from Geneva won a seat in the Council of States for the first time. The **Green Liberals** returned to the Council of States after a break of eight years.

gewusst: Every canton has the same number of seats in the Council of States, no matter how many people live there; only the former half-cantons have one seat each.
The cantons of Jura and Neuchâtel elect their members of the Council of States by proportional representation.

teile.einleitung: The United Federal Assembly is the joint sitting of the National Council and the Council of States. It meets mainly for important elections, for example to elect the Federal Council and the federal judges. Then all 246 members of parliament sit in the same chamber.
wichtigste: The United Federal Assembly is the joint sitting of both chambers.
It has 246 members: 200 from the National Council and 46 from the Council of States.
It elects the Federal Council and the Federal Chancellor.
It also elects the judges of the Federal Supreme Court.
Every year it elects the President of the Confederation.
It sits in the National Council chamber in the Federal Palace.
It is chaired by the President of the National Council.

abschnitte.text: Normally the National Council and the Council of States debate separately in their own chambers. But for certain business they come together and form the **United Federal Assembly**. Then all 246 members have one vote each. Because the National Council has more members, it carries more weight.

Its most important task is electing the **Federal Council**. After the parliamentary elections every four years, all seven federal councillors are elected one by one in December. If someone steps down, there is a by-election. Whoever reaches the **absolute majority**, that is, more than half of the valid votes, is elected.

The United Federal Assembly also elects the Federal Chancellor. It also elects the judges of the **Federal Supreme Court** in Lausanne and of other federal courts. Every December it decides who will be President and Vice President of the Confederation the following year. In times of war it would also elect a **general** for the army.

It also decides on pardons and on disputes about which federal authority is responsible. It does not make laws, though; the two chambers do that separately. Sometimes it also meets for ceremonial occasions, for example for speeches by guests from abroad. These sittings are public and are broadcast on television.

The United Federal Assembly sits in the **National Council chamber**, because it is the largest chamber in the Federal Palace. The members of the Council of States then sit in special seats along the back wall. The sitting is chaired by the President of the National Council. On election days there is often great excitement, and the public galleries are full.

begriffe.erklaerung: The joint sitting of the National Council and the Council of States.
More than half of all valid votes.
The highest court in Switzerland, in Lausanne.
A punishment is cancelled or reduced.

gewusst: Federal Council elections are secret; the members of parliament write the names on ballot papers.
The United Federal Assembly last elected a general in 1939, namely Henri Guisan.
In Federal Council elections, people are sometimes elected who had not officially stood at all.

teile.einleitung: On 6 January 2021, supporters of the defeated US President Donald Trump forced their way into the Capitol in Washington. There, Congress was due to confirm Joe Biden's election victory. The event is regarded as a serious attack on American democracy.
wichtigste: On 6 January 2021 thousands of Trump supporters stormed the Capitol.
They wanted to stop the confirmation of the Electoral College votes.
Vice President Mike Pence chaired the session and refused to overturn the result.
The session was interrupted and continued during the night.
The House of Representatives started a second impeachment against Trump.
The Senate acquitted Trump in February 2021.
On 20 January 2025 Trump pardoned about 1500 of those involved.

abschnitte.text: After the **2020 presidential election**, **Congress** counts the votes of the **Electoral College**, that is, the electors. On **6 January 2021** thousands of people forced their way into the **Capitol**, the parliament building in Washington. The members of Congress had to be taken to safety. The session was interrupted and continued during the night. In the end **Joe Biden's** victory was confirmed.

Before the attack, Trump and many supporters spread the claim that the election had been **stolen**. Their slogan was **“Stop the Steal”**. There was no evidence of massive **election fraud**. Courts rejected most of the lawsuits against the election result.

As President of the Senate, the **Vice President** chairs the count. At that time this was **Mike Pence**. He refused to change the result in Trump's favour. That is why he was threatened by attackers and had to be taken to safety.

On **13 January 2021** the **House of Representatives** voted to begin **impeachment proceedings** against Trump for inciting an insurrection. It was his second **impeachment**. In the Senate in February 2021, **57 out of 100** senators voted guilty, including 7 Republicans. **67 votes** would have been needed for a conviction, so Trump was acquitted.

A **select committee** of the House of Representatives investigated the events from 2021 to 2022. It held public hearings and presented a **final report** at the end of 2022. Many of those involved were convicted by courts. After returning to office, Trump **pardoned** about 1500 of them on **20 January 2025**, and he commuted the sentences of 14 more. To this day the event is judged very differently in the USA.
